agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: DiabeticBrain: A Portable Nano-biosensing system for managing early onset Alzheimer’s in diabetic patients
descriptions: Over the past decade, the incidence and prevalence of dementias, notably Alzheimer’s disease (AD), have surged, posing a significant strain on health resources worldwide. AD is characterized by cognitive decline, neuronal loss, and abnormal plaque formation in the brain. With projections from the World Health Organization (WHO) indicating a doubling of the elderly population by 2050, predominantly in lower- and middle-income nations, the burden of dementia is set to escalate, particularly in developing countries. The associated costs are anticipated to skyrocket, reaching $2.8 trillion by 2030. Urgent action is imperative to ensure quality of life for affected individuals. Early diagnosis of AD is crucial, given the lack of effective treatments once the disease progresses. The link between diabetes (DM) and cognitive impairment has also garnered attention, with studies suggesting an increased risk of AD among diabetic patients. In Egypt, socio-demographic shifts have led to a rise in non-communicable diseases like diabetes, exacerbating healthcare challenges, particularly in rural areas. This project comprises a collaborative effort between Nile University and the University of Bath aiming to develop innovative technologies to prevent AD-related cognitive decline in diabetics, addressing a pressing societal and economic threat in Egypt.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Development of Diagnosis and Prognosis Model using Whole Slide Images (WSI)-based  biomarkers for personalised treatment in Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma
descriptions:
"Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is a cancer that disproportionately
affects low-and-middle-income countries (LMICs) in Southeast Asia (SEA)
especially the lower socioeconomic groups. The X chromosome is known
to confer different genetic effects to develop NPC. Despite advancement in
cancer targeted therapies, radiotherapy remains the standard of care for
NPC and the overall survival of NPC patients is poor. Recurrence and
distant metastasis rates after primary treatment range from 15% to 58%
and partly explains the sharp decline of relative survival for Malaysian NPC
Stage I patients from 94% in the first year to 67% in the fifth year. Palliative
chemotherapy is the only option for metastatic NPC and the
immunotherapy, toripalimab, has been just FDA-approved for recurrent and
metastatic NPC. However, besides AJCC cancer staging, no established
biomarker is available as companion diagnostic or prognostic markers.
We have developed sophisticated machine learning algorithms to enable
precise characterisation of disease morphological features (H&E slides)
and data mining of these features for the discovery of clinically relevant
biomarkers. Our associated partners are currently developing NPC
prognostic markers from RNA-seq of tissue samples (unpublished data). It
thus supports our hypothesis that employment of our digital pathology
expertise, in collaboration with associated partners that have established
long term studies in high-incidence NPC regions of Malaysia, may yield
increased understanding of NPC pathogenesis for development of
omic-based imaging biomarkers stratified based on biological sex, thus
contributing to improve patient management and survival.
The proposed approaches could lead to tests with shorter turnaround time
and more cost-effective than the genetic-based assays, which will reduce
health disparities and improve patient's outcome. These benefits are
anticipated to spill over to other high incidence NPC countries, especially
the LMICs in SEA."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Innovation in industrial wastewater treatment and water reuse
descriptions:
"There is a global need for breakthrough solutions to ensure a resilient
planet in the face of water scarcity, water pollution, energy scarcity, and
climate change. These challenges are acutely felt in Egypt which has relied
mainly on a single water source - the Nile - and which is lacking in
indigenous energy resources. In this proposal, academic and industrial
partners will work together to provide a water treatment solution that can
reliably remove a wide range of pollutants from industrial wastewater
effluents, thus providing alternative water resources and reducing the
environmental pressures of effluent disposal. Under the British Council
Newton-Mosharafa programme (2020/22), the UK-Egypt academic partners
established a fruitful collaboration which will here be taken a step further by
developing a robust solution for water treatment and reuse by various
industries. In collaboration with industrial partners, we will develop a
versatile, containerised water treatment system that can be economically
manufactured in Egypt. This system will comprise: (1) state-of-the art
ultrafiltration to remove colloidal material; (2) energy-efficient batch reverse
osmosis technology, invented at University of Birmingham and developed
by Salinity Solutions Ltd, UK; and (3) low-cost photocatalysis that is
energised by sunlight to break down micropollutants. By combining these
techniques, almost any water stream can be rendered clean and safe. The
system will be deployed and tested by National Research Centre in Egypt
and will be also highlighted at the level of authorities responsible for water
treatment and management. This will spur the uptake of the technology for
the benefit of industries that are increasingly challenged as regards
sourcing of water and disposing of effluents."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Screening impact of human genetic diversity on drug toxicity
descriptions: Human genetic diversity is most pronounced in Africa, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa and this has major implications for healthcare, both in Africa itself and across the ‘Global North’. For example, adverse reactions to drugs that were developed by major Pharma for patients in western countries, without taking genetic diversity into account, is a common problem in African populations. Furthermore, rare genetic variations in the Global North are often 10-100x more frequent in the African diaspora (Auton et al.  2015 “The 1000 Genomes Project Consortium. A global reference for human genetic variation.” Nature 526, 68–74. https://doi.org/10.1038/nature15393). Studying genetic and cellular tools derived from African populations thus presents a valuable opportunity to deliver major impact of global value by identifying and characterising underlying biochemical mechanisms affecting human health and variable drug responses. The University of Dundee team has recently developed innovative new laboratory approaches for addressing this challenge, by studying how human genetic diversity can lead to variability in cellular proteins and thus in responses to drugs in clinical use (Platani et al., PLoSONE 2025). This is based upon our data showing that human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) are, at least in part, avatars of their donors in terms of their genes and protein expression (Mirauta et al., eLife 2020). Further, our data showed that very many biochemical pathways and drug targets are expressed in pluripotent hiPSCs, which provide the most comprehensive cell model we know of for measuring a broad range of drug responses, using a novel laboratory screening platform we have developed (Platani et al., PLoSONE 2025). Using this screening platform, we have detected examples of reproducible, variable drug responses between iPS cell lines derived from healthy donors of northern European background. However, this has not yet been applied to hiPS cells derived from patients of African descent. This collaborative project with the Scholefield team in South Africa will pioneer the application of our biochemical screening methods and protein analysis capabilities to analyse iPS cell lines generated from sub-Saharan African donors. We will compare drug responses in iPS cells from European and African donors and use a range of validated protein analysis strategies to characterise cellular mechanisms affected by genetic variation in human populations that can lead to off-target drug effects and variable responses. In addition, this collaborative project will allow for visits to the UK by members of the South African team to receive training and knowledge transfer, facilitating their future ability to explore further how genetic variation impacts on human health and variable drug responses in Africa.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Entrepreneurial Learning at the Margins: Developing Enterprise Skills in the Informal Rural Economy. Unlocking Tomorrow's Talent
descriptions: This project is an international collaboration between the University of Leeds (UK) and the University of Pretoria (South Africa), exploring how people living in rural areas—particularly those who are marginalised or working outside the formal economy—can develop the skills, confidence, and support needed to improve their livelihoods via entrepreneurial learning. The project investigates how entrepreneurial skills can be developed and supported at the margins of the rural economy. It focuses on constrained rural actors such as subsistence farmers, informal agricultural workers, and others engaged in rural economic activity—many of whom are women. Specifically, it explores how rural individuals can build on what they are already doing: for example, how subsistence farmers might improve production or transition into more formal markets; how informal workers might apply intrapreneurial skills to gain more autonomy or upward mobility; and how those already active in small-scale enterprises can develop further. Key research questions include: What practical, social, or institutional barriers prevent rural individuals from becoming more entrepreneurial? How can constrained actors leverage entrepreneurship and intrapreneurship skills to achieve upward social mobility? And for those who have managed to progress despite constraints, what lessons can be learnt from their experiences? These exploratory research questions directly build on emerging discussions in the constrained rural entrepreneurship literature. We will conduct qualitative ethnographic fieldwork—using a multi-method approach (interviews, diary-keeping, observations, photographs)—in rural communities to explore these questions, understand the lived experiences of rural people, and identify where and how entrepreneurial learning takes place and how learning might be constrained. The project will engage with other stakeholders, including commercial farmers, supply chain actors, agricultural extension officers, and training providers to explore support systems and barriers to inclusion. A key supporting partner is South Africa’s Agricultural Research Council, which will assist with data collection and access to study participants. With its role in working with rural communities, the ARC will benefit from deeper insight into participants' lived experiences.  In addition to data collection, the project will run joint workshops, mentoring, and knowledge exchange activities to support early-career researcher development in both countries. These activities will offer practical experience in international collaboration, qualitative research, and rural engagement—while also shaping the project’s direction as it evolves. This collaboration aligns strongly with the ISPF theme Tomorrow’s Talent, exploring how marginalised rural actors can develop their potential, while also building capacity among early-career researchers in the UK and South Africa. It also supports South Africa’s strategic priorities in agricultural and rural development, informal livelihoods, and inclusive growth. Short- to medium-term impact: •   Rural stakeholders: The project provides a platform for sharing experiences, raising visibility, and informing more inclusive approaches to enterprise support. It will help rural individuals strengthen their livelihoods and connect to wider economic opportunities. •   The research community: The collaboration between the University of Leeds and the University of Pretoria will build lasting academic ties, support co-authored outputs, and offer early-career researchers valuable international experience, mentoring opportunities, and research dissemination beyond academia (via practitioner/policy reports, podcasts, events).

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Eco-Creative Nature-Inspired Innovation for Coastal Erosion Mitigation (Eco-NICE)
descriptions:
"This Eco-NICE project brings together a transdisciplinary and
gender-balanced team of internationally leading academics with combined
expertise in offshore, coastal, and subsea engineering, numerical and
physical models, environmental waves and vortex-induced vibrations, and
field/lab measurement.
We aim to enhance the coastal resilience in Thailand through a
nature-inspired innovative use of Artificial Mangrove Roots (AMR). By
designing AMR to mimic the natural flow-structure energy transfer
mechanisms of mangrove roots, AMR can effectively reduce the wave
energy impact and promote sediment deposition, addressing coastal
erosion and advancing shoreline rehabilitation.
Key aspects of Eco-NICE include:
1) Field Observation: Utilizing UAV-LiDAR technology, the project will
monitor coastal changes in the upper Gulf of Thailand where AMR devices
are implemented. By involving local communities, governmental bodies,
and policymakers, stakeholder workshops will assess the impact and
gather feedback on AMR applications.
2) Laboratory Experiment: In-house tests will be conducted in a wave basin
at Chulalongkorn University to understand shoreline responses to various
AMR configurations and wave conditions, based on stakeholders' inputs,
aiming to optimize AMR design for real-life coastal environments.
3) Numerical Modelling: To comprehend AMR's hydrodynamics and
fluid-structure energy transfer mechanisms, numerical models will be
developed at Newcastle University, studying AMR's irregular shapes and
flexible body-wave interactions, and exploring its role in coastal erosion
mitigation. Analysis tools will benefit AMR designers, developers and
operators.
4) Policy Development: Policy guidelines will be formulated to promote
ecologically friendly practices for sustainable coastal management.
Through workshops at local, national and international levels, Eco-NICE
aims to influence policy decisions to ensure broader applications and
impact of its findings."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Development of an Integrated Platform for Studying the Human Health and Environmental Impact of Micro/Nanoplastics: Human 3D-Tissue Model, Simulated G
descriptions:
"This proposal is focused on establishing a new research collaboration between Swansea University (SU), UK and The National Science and Technology Development Agency (NSTDA), Thailand to share knowledge and expertise that will allow the reciprocal expansion of research on both the human and environmental safety of micro and nano-plastics. This activity will bring together scientists at SU and the NSTDA to address issues of national importance, whether considered from health, social or economic perspectives.
Plastic pollution is a significant problem world-wide both to human health and the environment. Addressing plastic pollution requires a multi-faceted approach, that must include reducing plastic production, improving waste management, promoting recycling, and developing alternatives to plastic materials. Public awareness and international cooperation are crucial to mitigating the effects of plastic pollution and protecting both environmental and human health. These plastics are broken down into particles known as micro and nano-plastics (MNP). While there is growing evidence of the potential human health and environmental risks posed by MNP, further research is required to develop our understanding of the true human impact of MNP exposure,
The activity undertaken will include a series of research exchanges across senior staff and early career researchers. This will include both scoping visits and workshops to develop strong working relationships and for discussion on establishing a defined programme of collaborative research. This activity will result in the development of new joint research ventures and build capacity across the two institutes to internationalize areas of strength in SU and NSTDA’s existing funded portfolio of activities in more predictive human tissue culture technology development and safety assessment. The UK-based scientists will share their knowledge on advanced in vitro 3D toxicity testing methods, which the NSTDA scientists will be able to apply to their workflow. In parallel, the NSTDA scientists will share knowledge on their zebrafish model for toxicity testing, 3D intestinal model and their simulated gut model.
The scientific data generated from this project can inform stricter regulations for plastic production and waste management, safeguarding public health and fostering the development of more environmentally friendly alternatives. This initiative can support the creation new green businesses and jobs, particularly benefiting low-income populations. The project’s findings will generate valuable data for public awareness campaigns, promoting responsible consumer behaviour and a cleaner environment."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Biosensor nanoparticles-based point of care detection of animals persistently infected with pestiviruses (BioPesti)
descriptions:
"Pestiviruses, including Bovine viral diarrhoea virus, Border disease virus, and classical swine fever virus cause substantial economic losses in ruminants and swine worldwide. This is usually associated with a negative impact on sustainable food production, farmers’ livelihoods, and food security. 
Rapid diagnosis of pestiviruses is crucial for disease control, especially in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where local access to laboratory diagnostics is limited, and samples often need to be sent to central labs or abroad leading to delays in results. This leads to pathogen outbreaks in LMICs being underreported and only noticed when they have already had a major economic impact and have spread across larger areas and many farm systems. Effective pestivirus diagnostic is also necessary for surveillance and identifying persistently infected (PI) animals which are the key to controlling the spread of the disease. Lack of diagnostic tools and the use of time-consuming diagnostic procedures for pestiviruses usually result in uncontrolled use of antimicrobials and other chemicals to control the diseases and to reduce losses. This behaviour has a negative environmental impact leading to the emergence of antimicrobial resistance in addition to food safety and food security problems. 
This proposal directly addresses the need for a rapid, cost-effective point-of-care (POC) test capable of identifying different viruses responsible for pestivirus infections in bovine, porcine, and ovine species. This will facilitate the rapid elimination of animals that may spread diseases. 
This study will bridge the gap between the development and characterisation of monoclonal antibodies at APHA and the use of these mAbs in translational research in Egypt. The POC test will support surveillance, detection, culling of persistently infected animals, and identification of infection with different pestiviruses in non-traditional hosts. The test will be validated in-lab and on-farm and will be compared to the gold standard and conventional testing methods to evaluate its analytical and operational performance. 
The development and deployment of biosensor nanoparticle-based assay will offer new diagnostic solutions for fast, portable, affordable testing on farms. The novel POC tests will improve infection management, livestock health and welfare, reduce inappropriate antimicrobial use, and enhance productivity. Developing PoC detection for pestiviruses will also enhance animal health surveillance and eradication of PI from cattle herds. With the rapidly declining cost of nanotechnology,the novel POC test could be used at farm, market, and national levels for disease surveillance. This approach will provide opportunities for enhanced integration of information about Pestiviruses in different hosts that would improve the control of the diseases and reduce their spread among and between different animal species. 
The proposed project will enhance the collaboration between APHA and Egyptian partners, a partnership that started more than 10 years ago through capacity building for laboratory diagnosis of Foot and mouth disease funded by EuFMD in 2012 and a workshop funded by Newton-Mosharafa Researcher Links Programme entitled “Controlling viral infections to improve food security and the nutrition of Egypt’s poorest communities” in 2016."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Air Quality Improvement and Resilience through Urban Morphology and Environment
descriptions:
"The project addresses a pressing issue in Southeast Asia (SEA): the high
risk of deteriorating air quality and escalating heat stress in cities, notably
Bangkok, Ho Chi Minh City and Manila, from 2010 to 2020. This rising
concern, with almost doubling the heat and air quality stress areas in
Manila, is linked with a significant research gap: while existing studies have
focused on identifying air pollutants and their sources, such as vehicular
emissions and industrial activities, there's a critical lack of insight into how
urban morphology and configuration directly influence air pollution levels
and public health. The variation in air quality and heat stress in different
cities, attributed to diverse urban parameters, has led to a doubling of
pollution and poor air quality, exacerbating urban heat island
characteristics.
By analyzing Manila's unique urban layout, the project will assess how
urban morphology and configuration impact on poor air quality and
increase heat stress in Manila cities over the last decade, namely: a)
identify different parameters to air quality variations in cities and b)
Combine UHI characteristics with distribution patterns to address pollution
and poor air quality to. This involves combining field evaluations with
parametric analysis to pinpoint factors exacerbating UHI effects. The
objective is to understand the relationship between urban form, air quality,
and public health, offering actionable urban planning insights to improve air
quality and reduce heat stress.
Outcomes include actionable recommendations and a deeper
understanding of how urban design affects environmental health. Through
detailed insights and practical recommendations, the study contributes to
society and the economy by promoting public health and fostering more
livable cities across Southeast Asia and beyond, addressing the urgent
need for innovative NBS intervention urban environments that support both
sustainable development and the health of their inhabitants."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Developing Educators' Competencies in Utilising Generative AI in Teaching and Learning through a Serious Game in Vietnam (GameAid)
descriptions:
"GameAid aims to support educators in Vietnam to develop awareness,
experience, and understanding of Generative AI (GenAI) in Education
through designing, prototyping, and evaluating a serious game. Embracing
teaching and learning with the use of GenAI tools, such as large language
models (LLMs) exemplified by ChatGPT, presents an overwhelming
decision for educators in Vietnam, impacting their digital literacy and ability
to personalise students learning experiences.
Vietnam's educational landscape is evolving with policies promoting
educational technology, including online assessments, and digital
resources, facilitating flexible learning. However, challenges persist,
including educators' lack of digital skills and their inability to design quality
learning resources. The 2020 survey on digital transformation in Vietnam
revealed that only 40% of teachers feel confident integrating technology
into teaching, and just 25% reported adequate training on digital tools.
Vietnam ranks 74th out of 133 countries in the Global Talent Competitive
Index, highlighting the urgent need for digital literacy development,
especially through purposeful media like serious games.
Recognising the vital link between educators' digital skills and teaching
quality, GameAid prioritises educators' experiences of using GenAI for
enhancing instruction. It incorporates the OpenAI API in a serious game for
demonstrating how teaching and learning can utilise GenAI. The serious
game will incorporate relevant content ranging from GAI applications and
tools and implications for teaching and learning (e.g. ethics, diversity, and
inclusivity) to designing digital content, learning activities, assessment, and
feedback. Moreover, through GameAid, educators will be supported via a
GenAI competency model and a centralised online hub for enhancing their
GenAI understanding, fostering meaningful, accessible, and inclusive
digital resources for leveraging teaching and learning with the use of
GenAI."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Intelligent Health Monitoring of Hydrogen Energy Components under Variable Operating Conditions
descriptions: The proposed collaborative research between the University of Huddersfield (UK) and Mansoura University (Egypt) addresses the ISPF themes of ’Resilient Planet’ and ’Transforming Technology’. This research endeavours to develop an industry-grade intelligent structural health monitoring (SHM) solution for rapid, remote, real-time monitoring, and future prognostics of Hydrogen Energy Components, including pressure vessels, valves, and pipelines, under variable loading and operating conditions. The primary goal is to utilize acoustic emission (AE), non-linear/linear ultrasonic guided wave (GW) propagation, and vibration-based sensing techniques to identify and characterize damages like hydrogen embrittlement, cracks, leakage, wear, and corrosion/oxidation under diverse environmental and operational conditions, including internal and external pressure, temperature, abrasion, and vibrations. This comprehensive approach includes prognostics under uncertain operating conditions such as temperature, vibration, and pressure, amalgamating rigorous experimental, analytical, and computational efforts. Moreover, the research integrates Bayesian data assimilation, and physics -based machine learning models, including Transfer-learning for adapting to real operating conditions and enabling future predictions. Critical to this initiative is the utilization of edge computing-based smart sensing technologies, enabling real-time wireless data sensing, acquisition, and transmission. The successful implementation of this proposal will enhance safety of Hydrogen energy systems through refinements in design and significantly reduce costs associated with maintenance, repair, and replacement. Furthermore, this excellent collaborative effort between the UK and Egypt holds promise in providing industries with intelligent condition monitoring technologies, thereby potentially revolutionizing operational practices. This research will significantly benefit from the expertise of leading industry collaboraters like KOSO Kent Introl (official Associated Partner, LoS attached), ITP Aero (existing collaborator, agreed but LoS could not processed due to a short notice), and MISTRAS Group (existing collaborator since 2021).

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: A Sustainably Resourced Advanced Coacervate Material Platform for Rapid Detection of Bacteria
descriptions: This is a basic research project in developing a novel material based on a sustainably sources natural biopolymer for rapid identification of bacteria. It focuses on the ISPF thematic priority area (for Turkey) of Healthy People, in relation to enhancing “Pathogen Detection” for tackling “Antimicrobial Resistance” (AMR) specifically, and “Global Health and Pandemics” more generally. The project will consist of both a programme of scientific experimental research and a programme of developmental activities based on boosting the future research, economic, and healthcare capacity of the partner country Turkey.     AMR poses a significant public health threat due to the overuse and misuse of antimicrobial agents, leading to multidrug-resistant strains. Fast, reliable bacterial detection is essential for combating AMR, allowing for accurate diagnosis and optimal antimicrobial prescription. This is emphasized by by the Strategic Research and Innovation Agenda on Antimicrobial Resistance (SRIA) of the international Joint Programming Initiative on Antimicrobial Resistance (JPIAMR), which includes Turkey and the UK.    The scientific programme will build on a range of recent research developments pioneered by the UK and Turkish project leaders. It will demonstrate a novel bacteria sensing material for automatic labelling bacteria by combining the bacteria-binding functionality of a biomimetic antimicrobial “peptoid” and the ability of a polymeric “coacervate” material to controllably release bioactive molecules. The proposed detection scheme will be more convenient, rapid, portable, and lower cost than current laboratory techniques requiring overnight or longer analyses.     The project will immediately benefit the partner countries by enabling additional scientific training, increased achievements of project researchers, and hence enhanced national research capacities. The impact will be demonstrated by research publications and conference presentations. The future projects that these results catalyse and the associated additional funding they attract then enhance the scientific landscape in the medium to long terms.    For the developmental programme, in addition to researcher training, the project leaders will deliver public outreach as well as organise a main engagement meeting with academic and industry researchers and a range of stakeholders. Additional, smaller consultative meetings are also anticipated. Outreach will in the immediate term educate the public of AMR and sustain interest in relevant research funding. The research user and stakeholder engagement will help develop plans for advancing the proposed technology and identifying the sources of future investments/funding required. The project leaders have already identified a range of stakeholder including clinicians, potential public and private funders, and existing European/UK and Turkish professional networks invested in promoting enhanced bacteria sensing applications.     Investors and public research funders understand that each novel biomedical technology takes sustained research and development. The support pledged by the project’s non-academic associated partners already indicates the potential of the project’s technology. By brining like-minded researchers and stakeholders together, the engagement meetings can already start catalysing additional healthcare, research and commercialisation ideas unrelated to the proposed project. In the longer term, the engagement, supported by the project’s novel scientific results, will catalyse the development of the proposed rapid bacteria identification technology for combatting AMR and advance healthcare in UK and Turkey.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Reducing impacts on elephants from construction of the Pan-Borneo Highway in Sabah
descriptions:
"The impacts of Linear Transport Infrastructure (LTI) development on Asian
elephants are a growing source of concern. The Pan Borneo Highway
(PBH) is Malaysia's biggest and most ambitious infrastructure project.
Several stretches in Sabah will bisect between 30 and 170 km of forest
reserves, potentially having devastating consequences for elephant
residents in the Central Sabah Managed Elephant Range (MER). This
project responds to the urgent need for proactive action to minimize and
mitigate these threats. We will carry out field studies using satellite imaging,
radio collaring, grid-based sign sampling, camera traps, and field
observation to provide reliable baseline data on how Bornean elephants
(Elephas maximus borneensis) currently use the area that the construction
of the road will impact. We will use the data to conduct a vulnerability
analysis to assess how elephants are likely to be impacted by the highway.
Comparison of survey data on elephant distribution and habitat use with the
projected extent of habitat degradation/destruction at different project
stages will identify critical risk areas and periods for other elephant groups
and individuals. The results will be disseminated to policymakers,
conservationists, and the general public in Sabah as input for
evidence-based decision-making, as well as to the scientific community
and conservation practitioners in Asian elephant range states. Our findings
will contribute to the definition of elephant-safe working practices during the
construction of the road and the identification of practical measures to
facilitate elephant movements and mitigate threats. We will engage in
dialogues with all responsible government agencies to ensure that our
findings are incorporated into the design of mitigation measures. The
project will train people in the area who encounter elephants on how to
respond to conflict and continue the slow but vital process of generating
public support for elephant conservation in Sabah."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Development of community-driven machine learning tools for the agri-tech sector in the Philippines.
descriptions:
"Many Filipino farmer (34%) live in poverty and the farming population is
ageing quickly, with an average age of 57 (it was 44 in the 1970s). A critical
shortage of farmers is expected in the next 15 years, impairing the
Philippines' ambition for self-sufficiency, and putting the farming sector at
risk. Solutions are required to modernise farming, improve efficiency,
upskill and to recruit new generations of farmers.
The ability of Filipino farmers to leverage modern precision agriculture
techniques is challenged by the fact that farms are small-scale. The costs
and efforts required for farmers to acquire, deploy, and leverage these
technologies are too high, even if these tools ultimately decrease costs,
increase production and appeal to the younger generation. Some farming
communities, such as the Santo Niño community, operate a co-operative
model. These community-driven organisations allow farmers to better
negotiate prices, provide loans, and they are effective means of
disseminating information and training. We argue that cooperatives can
also provide the critical mass required to stimulate precision agriculture
techniques in small scale farming.
We propose to work with the Santo Nino farming cooperative to develop
bespoke instruments and computational tools that integrate high-resolution
imagery collected by unmanned aerial vehicles to prototype precision
agriculture applications tailor-made for these small-scale producers,
targeting high-value crops grown in this representative community.
Algorithms created will be further calibrated and validated with concurrent
supporting field measurements, including from a purpose-built affordable
portable spectrometer.
By developing specially tailored yet transferable precision agriculture
solutions, we will assess the readiness level, knowledge gaps, training
needs, gauge acceptability and measure the value of these new
technologies to rural communities, and upskill a critically ageing sector of
the economy."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Quantum dots-based nano-optical antennas for versatile and sustainable agriculture
descriptions:
"The impact of climate change and the destruction of agricultural land due to
exponential population growth demand sustainable and efficient agricultural
practices to meet ever-increasing food demands. Plant growth can be
enhanced through artificial augmented photosynthesis by tailoring light for
different crops. Nanomaterials can be harnessed to convert higher,
harmful, or unused light frequencies to lower, photosynthetically useful
frequencies, thereby potentially increasing crop yields by around 20-50%.
However, currently available nanomaterials are often expensive, toxic,
and/or inefficient.
In this project, we aim to establish an academic partnership to address the
most challenging societal problems of food shortages, cost of living crisis,
and environmental issues faced by the world. Our ultimate goal is to
develop low-cost, non-toxic, and highly efficient spectral converters to
enhance the process of photosynthesis in plants. To achieve this, we will
design and synthesize highly efficient carbon quantum dots (CQDs) with
good absorbance in both the UV and NIR regions, long excited state
lifetimes, and high photoluminescence quantum yields. These CQDs will be
capable of efficient down- and uplight conversion, thus harnessing solar
light beyond the visible spectrum. We plan to utilize these CQDs as
nano-optical antennas via soil drenching or seed coating for delivery
through roots or via foliar spraying on leaves, or to incorporate them into
polymer films for use as a retrofit solution for greenhouse glazing or in
polytunnel plastics. This ambitious project aims to achieve greater than
50% photosynthesis efficiency and ultimately increase crop yields by more
than 20%.
The findings of the project will be shared with relevant parties, including
agricultural organizations, and will be disseminated through publications in
prestigious journals to increase the impact of outputs in a timely manner."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Soil Microbial diversity as a nature-based solution to improve climate resilience of rice production in the Lower Mekong  Basin (LMB)
descriptions:
"The Lower Mekong Basin (LMB), known as the region's rice basket, faces
challenges as rice yields remain low due to climate change induced
temperature & water stress. These factors threaten livelihoods & food
security in a region where rice production provides a staple food source,
labour & income (for 80% of population).NPU&NIAB will undertake this
project by collaborating with a previously established network of rice
cooperatives who actively engage innovative farmers of different
socio-economic backgrounds, female farmers & young farmers. Inequalities
in regional investment into irrigation infrastructure impacts how wealth is
distributed among the farming community. This provides a unique
opportunity to study microbial diversity in water-stressed conditions vs
irrigated. This study will quantify how environmental changes affect
microbial function & develop strategies to increase resilience in LMB. We
will assess & culture microbial populations adapted to water-stress for
future amendment candidates to reduce the effect of water-stress,
providing resilience to climate change. Previously a NIAB/NPU project
(Newton-527396167) isolated native microbes from the LMB and
developed prototype amendments. NIAB recently demonstrated increased
rice yield in Africa when combining Trichoderma with other BCA's.
Combinations of the prototype product and Trichoderma will be tested in
demonstration commercial farms, in association with the cooperatives.
Local events will showcase the benefits to a wide reach of LMB farmers.
Results will be used to inform farmers, local government & policy makers
on best practise, optimising natural resources & investment in infrastructure
to improve the prosperity and lives of the local population.
The project brings together Thai & UK researchers giving the opportunity
for knowledge & technology transfer & capacity building to ensure networks
for younger generations of researchers & farmers, future-proofing
sustainable agriculture in Thailand."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: SMART-COAT Sustainable Mitigation of Air Pollution and Resilience through Thermal-regulating COATings
descriptions: Air pollution is one of the most serious public health and environmental challenges of our time. In major cities around the world, including Bangkok, fine particles known as PM2.5 and toxic volatile organic compounds (VOCs) come from traffic, construction sites, and industrial emissions. These pollutants harm human health and contribute to the formation of smog and the urban heat island effect. Existing pollution mitigation strategies are often expensive, difficult to scale, and reactive rather than preventive.There exists a critical gap in the availability of passive, low-cost, and easily deployable technologies that can be integrated directly into urban infrastructure, remain effective under high humidity and solar variability, and address both air quality and thermal stress.  This project will address this gap through the formulation of a novel multifunctional photocatalytic paint that integrates visible-light active photocatalysts (enabling activity under ambient sunlight, unlike traditional UV-dependent systems), biochar-based sorbents for enhanced PM2.5 adsorption, and anti-static, self-cleaning additives to minimise dust accumulation and sustain long-term efficacy. Additionally, the paint includes infrared-reflective pigments to reduce solar heat absorption, thus offering local cooling benefits. This unique combination of properties enables the paint to provide both air purification and thermal mitigation, offering a practical and scalable solution for cities facing pollution and climate challenges. The overarching aim is to translate this innovation from laboratory to real-world urban application. Specific objectives include: (1) optimising the multifunctional paint formulation for durability and performance under tropical climatic conditions. (2) monitoring PM2.5 and VOC reduction in situ using sensor networks. (3) co-developing policy guidance with local stakeholders to support the adoption of photocatalytic paint technologies within urban planning frameworks, building regulations, and air quality management strategies. This will be achieved through first, developing and laboratory testing paint samples under controlled conditions, and then large scale trials to prove real-world performance. This collaboration unites the University of Surrey, renowned for its advanced air quality monitoring, urban environmental modeling and public health impact assessment, with King Mongkut’s University of Technology Thonburi (KMUTT), which brings expertise in materials chemistry and paint formulation. Complementing these academic strengths, a leading Thai paint company ensures the project's industrial feasibility, scalability, and potential for successful commercialisation. This trilateral partnership will allow us to co-develop, test, and implement a solution that is both technically innovative and regionally appropriate. By the end of the project, we expect to deliver a validated, field-tested photocatalytic paint with demonstrable efficacy in pollutant removal and surface cooling. It offers a low-cost, scalable, and climate-resilient technology that can be implemented throughout Southeast Asia. By engaging with environmental agencies, city planners, and community organisations, in the short term, it will reduce local exposure to air pollution. In the medium term, it will inform urban planning, environmental regulation, and public health policy, creating pathways for replication in other cities across the region. By transforming ordinary walls into air-purifying, heat-reflecting surfaces, this project will demonstrate how innovative surface technologies can transform passive urban infrastructure into active tools for environmental protection and public health improvement.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Eco-friendly Hybrid Desalination System via integrating Solar and Geothermal Energy with Biomaterials
descriptions:
Scientists have made progress in developing Adsorption Desalination (AdsDes) technology to meet Egypt’s freshwater shortage with minimal energy demand. One of the main advantages of AdsDes is its ability to operate at low temperatures, therefore waste heat or renewable energy sources like solar or geothermal energy can be utilised as the energy source. Another advantage is its capability to produce cooling alongside water desalination. However, several technical challenges hinder its broad utilisation, which we aim to address through a team effort to take further steps in transforming AdsDes technology. Besides, we will work with other societal organisations to address the social inclusion challenges that promote broad access to such technology. 

By integrating cutting-edge renewable energy technologies, we aim to revolutionise the efficiency and sustainability of water desalination in Egypt. For the first time, we will hybridise multiple renewable resources, primarily solar (thermal and PV) and geothermal, and utilise the soil as a heat storage medium to maintain the 24/7-year-round of the AdsDes system. Using multiple renewable resources will enable us to develop closed cooling and heating circuits without additional water supplies to provide the required heating and cooling for the system’s operation. We will leverage the emerging locally available biomass to develop a low-cost adsorption composite comprising biochar and salt hydrates. 

This timely project contributes to achieving sustainable development goals (SDG5, SDG6, SDG7, SDG11, and SDG17) and aligns with Egypt’s 2030 vision.

The project will study geothermal and solar energy integration to power the AdsDes system. MATLAB and TRNSYS software will be used to simulate and optimise the system’s design and performance. Additionally, CFD (Computational Fluid Dynamics) simulations will be employed to analyse the fluid flow and heat transfer within the AdsDes system core components, providing detailed insights into its operational efficiency and identifying potential areas for improvement for optimal component-to-system level operation. Sustainable adsorption composites will be utilised to enhance the system economically. The techno-economic impacts will be benchmarked against existing technologies to appeal to investors. We will undertake educational and awareness campaigns targeting underrepresented groups in Egypt regarding the developed renewable-driven system.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Empowering Women in Legal Research for Democratic Resilience and Constitutional Renewal in Turkey
descriptions: This project will establish collaboration between the University of Essex and Sabancı University, Istanbul, to support women in legal studies during the current process of democratic erosion and constitutional change in Turkey. We aim to foster talent and impact by establishing a network of support for women legal scholars and by offering the necessary tools to make a meaningful intervention in society. The project will develop an innovative academic programme on constitutional rights and renewal, and produce proposals for gender equality, social rights, and civic empowerment. The aim of the partnership is to develop historically grounded, normatively robust, and development-relevant frameworks for democratic resilience through capacity-strengthening activities focused on civic empowerment, gender equity, and inclusive governance. Given the dismantling of constitutional safeguards and the resurgence of authoritarianism, rethinking basic laws in Turkey is critical. The shift from a parliamentary to a presidential system in 2018 entrenched executive dominance, marginalised the legislature, and curtailed judicial independence. As a result, individual rights, especially women’s rights, are being systematically eroded. This regression is further reflected in Turkey’s 2021 withdrawal from the Istanbul Convention, a landmark treaty on preventing gender-based violence, and the stagnation of the Gender Development Index over the past decade. With a new constitution on the future political agenda, a further centralisation of power and weakening of rights is expected.  The project has significant impact potential in the process of constitutional change in Turkey by empowering women in legal studies to develop innovative constitutional proposals. Drawing on the tradition of transformative constitutionalism, we will generate insights into democratic design under crisis conditions, enriching academic debates by offering practical pathways for lawmakers, judges, and civil society to shape a more inclusive and resilient constitutional framework. Key outcomes: UK–Turkey Summer School on constitutional resilience and gender-inclusive reform, which will culminate with students’ proposals for constitutional renewal joint curriculum development embedding constitutional themes into university teaching  public workshops hosted by Sabancı’s Istanbul Policy Centre establishment of a Turkish chapter of SAFI and hosting of the 2027 SAFI Conference in Istanbul, where student’s proposals for constitutional reform will be critically analysed by internationally renowned legal scholars one co-authored article on constitutional renewal in Turkey

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Supporting Tomorrow’s Talent by exploring entrepreneurial activities and innovation in the Kenyan informal economy
descriptions:
"This collaboration between the Universities of Nairobi and Leeds initiates research and a capacity-building research network that shines a light on entrepreneurial activities amongst the most vulnerable in society, who operate within what is known as the informal economy. This is the unregulated, untaxed economy most Kenyans interact with on a daily basis for income generation or sourcing everyday items. Understanding the nuanced dynamics of these entrepreneurs and their businesses is vital in working towards SDGs such as decent work or poverty alleviation.

This collaboration extends prior activities to facilitate the development of ”Tomorrow’s Talent” in a co-created manner, of a unique network of informal economy researchers from within Kenya, across Africa and globally. It utilizes a hybrid approach that mixes online capacity building and collaboration-building activities that facilitate widespread inclusion, with targeted developmental activities for Kenyan academics through in-person workshops, mentoring, staff exchanges and knowledge exchange.

The team will co-create new knowledge and theory on informal economy entrepreneurship through a set of fieldwork activities. The main element of this uses access to a unique group of women entrepreneurs who operate micro-bakeries in the informal economy. It researches their entrepreneurial ecosystem, experiences and facilitating factors to make critical contributions to our existing knowledge and theory base on entrepreneurship and innovations in such marginalized contexts. Working with this community also offers opportunities to explore aspects of food security in these vulnerable contexts.

The programme will have an impact both the short and medium term, on individuals, policy or practice, either directly through the targeted developmental activities or through impact generated through the research outputs of the collaborative team and the wider network."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Adapting crisis responses to salt-droughts in the Mekong Delta, Vietnam
descriptions:
"Floods have traditionally been an integral part of peoples' lives in the
Mekong delta in Vietnam. However, in 2016 and 2020 Vietnam
experienced major droughts, accompanied by increasing levels of salt
intrusion. These droughts are referred to as salt-droughts. The 2020
salt-drought caused five delta provinces to declare a state of emergency,
and was the worst drought on record since 1926. Accordingly,
technologies, knowledges, data and practices in government and local
communities on how to respond to droughts are still emergent.
This project will contribute to enhancing future resilience to salt-intrusion
and droughts in the Mekong delta, by bringing together diverse knowledges
held by government, local communities and researchers. By bridging
emergent and established understandings, and scientific/professional and
local/lay knowledges, the project will enable better long-term policy making
and the development of sustainable practices.
We will work at the commune level in the provinces of Soc Trang (Tran De,
Long Phu and Nga Nam districts) and Ca Mau (U Minh, Tran Van Thoi,
Thoi Binh and Cai Nuoc districts). These are amongst the most exposed
areas to salt-droughts. We will develop a pilot study that will lay the
foundation for the development of a drought early warning (monitoring and
forecasting) system in collaboration with our associated partners. We do
this by ground-truthing remote sensing and hydrometeorological, land use
and other technical data with community experiences, knowledges and
understandings on drought and salinity, applying a gender focus
throughout. Through this we will create dialogue on how different types of
data represent different knowledge and understandings of drought and
drought impact. This enables us to develop capacity for community
engagement and decision-support, and to develop the information basis for
the development of solutions that benefit local livelihoods."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Development and field testing of real-time Artificial Intelligence Early Warning System to help increase safety for people and elephants in shared lan
descriptions:
"This proposal seeks to develop state-of-the-art real time Artificial Intelligence edge-computing devices that leverage on deep learning technologies for the detection and behaviour study of wild elephants in human-elephant shared landscapes. This proposed project leverages on experts in the field of elephant research, human-wildlife conflict management, wildlife conservation and computer technology at the Zoological Society of London and University Malaysia Pahang. 
Human-wildlife conflict poses significant challenges to both agricultural sustainability and wildlife conservation efforts. In the case of wild Asian elephants (Elephas maximus), all 13 range countries with wild elephant populations are facing human-elephant conflict whereby annually, an estimate of more than 600 human lives and 450 elephants were killed due to the conflict. By integrating advanced computer vision techniques and audio bioacoustics analysis, and through the implementation of deep learning algorithms, this project aims to facilitate a more peaceful human-elephant coexistence by increasing safety for both people and elephants. Suitable and comparable study sites will be selected covering wild habitats for elephants and agriculture areas, with focus on human-wildlife conflict sites in Malaysia and Thailand. The research will involve data collection to train A.I. algorithms, hardware development, and deployment of innovative edge-computing devices in the target areas, while enabling the continuous collection of vision and audio data for studying elephant behaviour patterns. The outcomes of this research have the potential to significantly impact wildlife conservation efforts, community wellbeing, and agricultural sustainability in regions affected by human-elephant conflict, promoting coexistence. Furthermore, the development of these advanced edge-computing devices holds promise for broader applications in wildlife research, monitoring, and conflict management."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Inclusive use of Artificial Intelligence in education in Vietnam: AI powered inclusive education digital transformation in rural and urban schools
descriptions:
"This interdisciplinary project aims to address the digital transformation
across Vietnam focussing on developing practices with educators and
learners from diverse geographic areas and different gender groups across
Vietnam on the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools for teaching and
learning (T&L). Recent proliferation of the use of AI in education has
coincided with the Vietnam Government's decision on ""a national digital
transformation programme until 2025 orientation to 2030""
(Decision749/QD-TTg 2020). Inclusivity is identified as a key area of digital
transformation for education prioritising providing schools and pupils in
rural areas with access to the latest digital technologies and to develop
digital literacy and competencies for teachers and pupils from different
gender groups (Anh Vinh et al 2023; Dang Dao et al 2022).
This project involves education and computer science researchers from the
UK (BCU, NTU) and Vietnam (HCMUE, HUE, VNU, VU) working with
schools and educators in Vietnam to co-develop pedagogical practices and
resources to trial latest AIEd technologies. Three bespoke tools,
conversational AI, large language models and a multimodal affect
recognition system will be piloted with educators and learners from six
schools. The project focuses on the pedagogical experiences,
considerations and needs from rural and urban areas in Vietnam with the
aim to learn about the perspectives of educators and learners from different
gender groups from these areas on using AI in education. This is
underpinned by UNESCO's recommendation (2019) that 'as AI is
emerging, there is an opportunity to involve education stakeholders at an
early stage to shape them based on educators', learners' and education
leaders' perspectives for sustainable development and implementation of
AI'. Project findings will be developed into resources for educators and
researchers; and inform a roadmap and recommendations for a sustainable
development of emerging tech for education."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Quantum Dots for Photosynthesis Enhancement In Cereals (QUPEC)
descriptions:
"Rice serves as a staple food for billions in Asia, but current production
methods struggle to keep pace with population growth. Enhancing rice
photosynthesis, the fundamental process driving carbohydrate production,
offers a promising avenue to significantly increase yield in
carbohydrate-rich plants like rice. Quantum Dots (QDs) are nanomaterials
with unique photoluminescent properties. Unlike traditional methods that
focus on nutrient manipulation, QDs offer a novel approach to improve crop
yields, by increasing the photosynthetic efficiency within the plant itself.
In our previous work, biocompatible QDs were successfully prepared from
agriculture waste. We found that different agriculture waste materials
produce QD with different properties. However, despite the empirical
evidence supporting the potential of QDs, the mechanism of
photosynthesis enhancement remains unclear, and the plant molecular and
biochemical responses to QDs are unknown Addressing this knowledge
gaps is essential for developing effective QD-based applications for
photosynthesis enhancement in paddy rice.
This research proposes to address 3 key research questions:
1) Impact of source waste materials: How do different sources impact QD's
photoluminescence and photosynthesis enhancement properties?
2) Mechanism of Photosynthesis Enhancement: How do different QDs
improve photosynthesis in plants, and what are the underlying
mechanisms? What alterations happen in the photosystems and related
biochemical and molecular pathways after exposure to QD?
3) Optimising QD Concentration: What is the ideal concentration of QDs to
maximize photosynthesis enhancement in paddy?
By elucidating biochemical response to QDs, this research endeavours to
improve current agricultural practices and alleviate the global food market
pressures, building sustainable agricultural solutions for a resilient planet."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Beta-Lactam Resistant Strain Replacement of Zoonotic Streptococcus suis in Slaughtered Pigs from Thailand: Global Risks to Food Security and Public He
descriptions:
"Streptococcus suis is a pig respiratory commensal but often causes
invasive disease in pigs and in humans who have pig-related occupations
or consume raw pork. In Thailand, human S. suis infection mainly results
from consumption, but despite public health campaigns promoting pork
cooking, disease incidence hasn't decreased.
Most disease-causing isolates of S. suis come from a few genetic lineages,
with one, CC1, causing most zoonotic infections. These lineages are
susceptible to beta lactams, but commensal lineages already show
beta-lactam resistance. Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) mechanisms could
easily spread to pathogenic lineages via recombination in highly competent
S. suis. As S. suis infection in both pigs and humans is almost exclusively
controlled with beta-lactams, this poses a considerable food security and
public health risk.
Genetic surveillance of S. suis in Thai humans has revealed the
emergence of a new zoonotic lineage with reduced susceptibility to beta
lactams. As human isolates originate in pigs, we hypothesise a population
shift of S. suis in Thai pigs, supported by evidence of rising AMR levels in
diseased pigs. However, genomic surveillance of S. suis is lacking from the
source of human infection - slaughtered pigs - leaving a critical research
gap. Targeting S. suis in slaughtered pigs is vital for safeguarding human
health. Moreover, beta-lactam-resistance in a pathogenic lineage poses a
global food security risk, should it spread more widely.
This project aims to determine the prevalence and genomic epidemiology
of pathogenic and zoonotic S. suis lineages in slaughtered pigs, identify the
genetic basis of beta-lactam resistance in Thai isolates and determine how
resistance mechanisms spread. Our goal is to enhance capability and
technological capacity in AMR surveillance in Thailand, guide treatment in
pigs and humans, and communicate evidence-based AMR trends to
stakeholders in policy, farming and medicine."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Indo-NATAL - Indonesia National Birth and Early-life Tracking
descriptions:
"Indonesia, the world's fourth most populous country, has over 271 million
people with diverse cultures and geography (1) and faces a vast number of
health challenges. Some of the major challenges lie in the areas of
maternal and child health (2), including malnutrition and stunting which lead
to various chronic health problems later in life. Despite its size and
diversity, Indonesia has limited participation and representativeness in
global health research.
As the understanding of the significance of the life course expands, the
importance of birth cohort studies is increasingly recognized. However,
there is a lack of comprehensive, large-scale cohort studies in Indonesia,
which represents a significant limitation in understanding these diverse
health issues. Bringing together regional birth cohorts could establish a
robust platform for investigating health outcomes and risk factors in later
life, and interventions on a national scale.
Currently there are a few existing longitudinal studies, including Indonesian
Family Life Survey (IFLS) and Summit Institute for Development (SID).
However, both the IFLS and SID were not specifically designed as birth
cohorts. In addition, while IFLS has a diverse coverage, it mostly focused
on household survey. The SID focuses on a micronutrient supplementation
trial and is only conducted in one small island in Indonesia (Lombok, Nusa
Tenggara Timur).
We propose a platform of a national birth cohort titled ""Indonesia National
Birth and Early-life Tracking"" abbreviated as ""IndoNATAL"". Learning from
ongoing UK birth cohort studies (3)(4), our strategy involves leveraging
expertise and platforms from existing cohorts in the UK and Indonesia to
create a collaborative birth cohort in Indonesia, forming nationally
representative samples. Collaborative partnerships between health facilities
and academic/research groups in the UK and Indonesia are crucial to
facilitate study implementation to better understand health over the
life-cours"

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Monitoring Degradation and Recovery to Support Restoration of Vietnam's forests
descriptions:
"Forests in Vietnam face multiple stresses from climate change, logging and
hunting. Threats from climate change, particularly heat waves, droughts
and storms are intensifying. In an attempt to reduce forest degradation,
Vietnam has introduced logging bans, but unlicensed logging continues
and is widespread. It is not known if forests in Vietnam continue to be
degraded or if they have started to recover, with important implications for
forest resources and for the millions of rural poor who rely on the forests for
their livelihoods. It is important we understand the response of natural
forests in Vietnam to these stresses to inform future forest management
and restoration strategies. This proposal brings together a team of
world-leading researchers from Vietnam and the UK to improve our
understanding of the resilience of Vietnam's forests to climate change and
logging. We will synthesise data from existing forest surveys across the
country and conduct extensive field work to resurvey forest plots. New
information from these surveys will be combined with satellite remote
sensed data of forest disturbance to provide novel understanding on the
trajectory of forests in Vietnam. Workshops will help build networks,
exchange knowledge and strengthen capacity. Knowledge exchange with
policy and environmental NGOs will bolster forest landscape restoration
across Vietnam. Our proposal will initiate new research collaborations,
contribute to improved sustainable management of forests in Vietnam and
support Vietnam achieve its climate change and nature recovery
commitments."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Quantifying heavy metal storage, hydrological connectivity, and ecological risk in the Red River Delta, Vietnam
descriptions:
"The proliferation of urbanisation and industrial expansion in northern
Vietnam is increasing the discharge of pollutants into waterways. However,
to date no comprehensive assessment of how and where they deposit in
waterways exists. To address this, we will quantify the storage of toxic
heavy metals in lake sediments across the Red River Delta (RRD),
assessing current and past toxicity levels and their relationship with
hydrological connectivity. Heavy metals, from industrial wastewater and
agricultural fertilisers, pose significant health risks to aquatic biota, the
ecosystem services they provide, and human populations within the RRD.
However, there is limited understanding of the potential health risk
associated with these stores of metals and the impact that mobilisation or
disturbance from human activity or intensified rainfall events could have on
their release. An understanding is essential to better understand the future
health and sustainability of aquatic aquaculture and human population
health.
Chemical and hydroclimate fluctuations over the past ~100 years will be
reconstructed through the analysis of lake sediment cores from strategically
located sites across the RRD. This project will also validate the wider use
of oxygen isotopes in the RRD, particularly of ostracods (small bivalved
crustaceans preserved in sediment cores), to reconstruct past rainfall
patterns, connectivity with the river network, and assess this relationship
with reconstructed heavy metal toxicity.
The project will quantify 'baseline' toxicity pre-dating major industrialisation
in the catchment over the past 30 years, to inform pollution control policies
and aquatic restoration management. The project will have significant
implications for environmental management and sustainable development
in the RRD by facilitating informed decision-making processes for
mitigating environmental risks and promoting ecosystem health."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Zero emission cooling hub for small-scale fisheries
descriptions:
"Indonesia is the second largest seafood producer in the world and
geographically located in the tropics with an annual average air
temperature of 28 ?C. The need for suitable cold chain in food production is
clear, yet access to cold chain technologies is still lacking for small-scale
fishers, which account for 80% of fishermen/women in Indonesia. This
leads to a high number of food loss due to wasted catch and limited
economic opportunities due to inability to store the catch for longer periods.
The project will produce a techno-economic blueprint for zero emission and
affordable cooling hubs that can cover two main cooling services needed
by small-scale fisheries: cold storage and ice making. The cold storage
service will be used to store the fish catch on shore, while the ice-making
service will be used to produce ice block or slurry for onboard cold storage
in the fishing boat. Two case studies have been identified in preliminary
engagement with local stakeholders: Bungin Island, West Nusa Tenggara
and Liran Island, Southwest Maluku.
The research work will focus on two main aspects of the cooling hub: (i)
design and optimisation of energy technologies that provide the cooling
services, and (ii) design and optimisation of the cold storage itself.
Considered energy technologies include solar photovoltaics, biogas,
natural refrigerant chillers, thermal energy storage, and batteries. The cold
storage will be designed to be able to store different seafood and farm
products at different temperature levels. Multi-objective optimisation will be
performed to balance the technical, financial, and environmental aspects.
Furthermore, viable business models will be co-developed with local
stakeholders to improve affordability and acceptability of the cooling hub
solutions."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Exploring Virome Diversity Among Domestic and Wild Birds in Live Bird Markets: Advancing Disease Outbreak Prediction Through Viral Metagenomics.
descriptions: The proposal directly addresses several development challenges faced by Egypt in the realm of poultry production and public health. Firstly, the sudden emergence of avian viral diseases has significantly impacted poultry production, increased production costs, and reduced profits. Many of these viral diseases are introduced to Egypt through direct contact between wild and domestic birds, highlighting the need for a better understanding of the virome in wild birds. The current traditional diagnostic tools have limited effectiveness in surveilling wild birds due to the wide diversity of viruses they can silently harbor during migration, coupled with the unpredictable emergence of pathogens and the influence of climate change on disease spread patterns. This may lead to the silent introduction and spread of virus infections. Secondly, the high prevalence of AMR bacteria is a major threat to public health in Egypt, with wild birds playing a crucial role in the dissemination of AMR bacteria that can be increased due to, at least partially, immunosuppression associated with the presence of certain immunosuppressive viruses. To address these challenges, we propose utilizing a metagenomic approach to investigate viral communities in wild and domestic birds in LBMs and correlating these results with AMR profiling. By investigating viromes in unique hotspots like LBMs, we aim to gain insights into the unique and shared viral pathogens between wild and domestic birds during close contact. This approach will provide valuable data that has not been previously available for developing diagnostic approaches to mitigate future outbreaks spread by wild birds globally. Furthermore, by understanding this diversity and correlating it with the current national and global virus situation, we can develop more efficient diagnostics targeting important diseases for routine diagnosis and improve our preparedness by identifying and developing tools to control unexpected pandemics.  In Egypt, poultry meat serves as the primary source of animal protein, accounting for approximately 44% of the locally consumed animal protein. Alongside the 1.4 million individuals engaged in the Egyptian commercial poultry sector, there are also five to seven million households involved in household poultry production (HHPP). HHPP plays crucial social, economic, and cultural roles in rural communities. All these stakeholders directly benefit from any effort to control viral outbreaks that have a devastating impact on their production. Our proposed approach aims to develop tools to effectively diagnose, predict and subsequently better ability to manage unexpected pandemics, thereby safeguarding the poultry industry from sudden viral infection emergence or minimizing its impact. Additionally, by enhancing the capacity of the RLQP in Egypt through training in HTS and bioinformatics analysis and data management, we will contribute to the development of local expertise and infrastructure for disease surveillance and control. This will not only improve the country's preparedness for future disease outbreaks but also create opportunities for local scientists to engage in cutting-edge research and contribute to global scientific knowledge. Furthermore, establishing robust networks for effective wild bird surveillance between the UK and Egypt will facilitate collaboration in research and diagnostics, particularly concerning viruses of global concern. This collaboration has the potential to attract additional funding and resources to Egypt, further supporting research and development activities in the country.  To deliver development impact within the project's lifetime and in the longer term, we will employ a multifaceted approach that involves collaboration with key stakeholders and beneficiaries. Our strategy includes: RLQP generates periodic reports on avian disease situations in Egypt, which are distributed to veterinary authorities, and major poultry producers in Egypt. We aim

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: BEST: Blended Education for STEM Teaching
descriptions:
"Engagement with science, engineering, technology and mathematics
(STEM) is increasingly important for the economic development and social
welfare that underpins a prosperous and healthy society. However, in many
countries including Malaysia, as students progress beyond primary school
their interest in STEM wanes
To counter this research has shown that a tangible, tactile and physical
learning experience - such as the BBC micro:bit, used by ~44M students
globally makes STEM subjects more engaging and promotes
problem-solving skills. Unfortunately, many OECD development assistance
committee (DAC) countries cannot use micro:bits; despite a relatively low
cost they rely on PCs which are uncommon in DAC schools. 'Unplugged'
activities, where students problem-solve with pencil-and-paper or via
playground-based physical activities, can be powerful but don't bring the
benefits of direct interaction with technology.
Project BEST leverages a new learning experience, MicroCode, where
students use a micro:bit without a costly PC to engage in problem-solving
activities that underpin STEM subjects. Working with local educators we
will adapt MicroCode, which has been validated in two UK schools, for use
in Malaysia. We will develop a blended transition from the unplugged
activities we have already run in the region, to provide a natural STEM
learning progression through lower secondary school, supporting students
as they elect subject specialisms.
Having evaluated and further refined MicroCode we will engage with
regional stakeholders to build a community of practice and lending library to
scale-up BEST to serve more low-income students. We believe that
MicroCode's low cost can provide a valuable pathway for teachers in DAC
countries to move beyond unplugged activities, leveraging positive emotion
to drive engagement and stretch students. Ultimately, we aim to level-up
the problem-solving abilities and STEM skills of students in low-income
communities across DAC countries"

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Development of an Egypt-UK collaborative research service to enable precision medicine and optimise outcomes for hypogonadism
descriptions:
Congenital Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism (CHH) is a rare, usually inherited, disorder caused by lack of reproductive hormones produced from the brain (gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) from the hypothalamus and/or gonadotropins from the pituitary gland). CHH includes Kallmann syndrome, where patients have no sense of smell (anosmia), and so-called idiopathic hypogonadotropic hypogonadism which typically presents with delayed or absent puberty. 
Individuals with severe, central disorders of this reproductive hormone axis, including CHH and combined pituitary hormone deficiency, are affected by underdeveloped genitalia, absent puberty, and long-term reproductive and fertility difficulties. Additionally, these disorders are associated with significant adverse health risks and serious psychosocial outcomes.
Identifying the genetic causes of CHH in children and adolescents is important for precision medicine and improvement of outcomes for patients. Upwards of 70 genes, mutations in which contribute to the development of CHH, have been identified. However, increasingly patients have more than one gene variant identified, and computational analysis may be insufficient to define if this gene or variant is the cause of their disease. Thus, establishment of infrastructure for additional laboratory analysis of genetic data is vital to establish if novel variants are disease-causing, in identifying the mechanisms of such genetic causes, and to guide in tailoring the treatment protocol for the individual patient across their life course. These challenges are particularly acute in resource-limited settings,such as our partner country of Egypt.
The management of infertility in patients with severe CHH is particularly challenging. In this patient group, hormonal therapy to promote sperm production is unsuccessful in up to 50% of adult men. This is largely due to lack of appropriate hormonal replacement in childhood. Additionally, these conditions carry a significant physical and psychosocial burden for patients and their families. Both men and women with GD report persistently high levels of anxiety, distress, depression and body shame, and low levels of confidence in relation to physical relationships. Thus, early and accurate diagnosis, with treatment guided to address the specific endocrine deficiencies of a particular patient, are needed to improve long-term outcomes.
