This proposed Egypt-UK collaboration will set up a well-structured pipeline across a national network for Egyptian patients with CHH, which will comprise identification and diagnostics, accurate genetic analysis with laboratory characterisation and promotion of up-to-date, optimised treatment protocols to improve reproductive and non-reproductive outcomes. We will promote best practice across national centres, to increase awareness, standardise diagnostic approaches, improve access to genetic testing and optimise output from genetic diagnosis to care for patients in the most appropriate manner for their particular disease. 
Accurate and proper genetic counselling for the affected families would help to identify these conditions earlier and reduce adverse health risks and social stigma, which will lead to a better quality of life for both the patients and their families. Moreover, this project is important for raising awareness across Egypt, and internationally, among paediatrician and clinicians about referral and diagnostic pathways and treatment protocols for patients with this condition.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Rationally designed vaccine production platform against FMDV
descriptions:
"Foot and mouth disease virus (FMDV) causes highly contagious and
economically destructive diseases in livestock (e.g. cattle) primarily in Asia,
Africa, and South America. Developed countries including the UK have
witnessed deadly outbreaks and remain on high alert due to the
infectiousness of the virus. The infamous FMDV outbreak started in the UK
in 2001 spread to many countries in Europe and led to £3.1 billion in losses
in the UK alone. The FMD is controlled predominantly by vaccination in
disease-endemic countries, however, due to diverse serotypes (n=7),
ineffective vaccines, and limited infrastructure to hold live FMDV, there is
an unmet continued need for novel vaccines that can be produced globally
and economically. In this proposal, we built a competitive consortium with a
range of existing tools and expertise to offer an economical, scalable, and
highly effective vaccine against FMDV.
We will first map the genetic and micro-antigenic diversity of the most
prevalent serotypes of FMDV using existing sample banks and targeted
sampling characterization using next-generation sequencing (Egypt). The
data-driven, field-informed, and high-resolution diversity of the FMDV will
guide the selection of representative strains and antigens for vaccine
construction (UK). In the second step, we will apply highly innovative
structure-guided and surface-charge condensation approaches to offer
novel, stable, and thermo-tolerant FMDV capsid proteins which will be
exploited to engineer virus-like particles (VLPs) in our in-house adapted
yeast expression system (UK). In the third step, fully characterized, highly
stable, and infectious VLP representing each of the prevalent serotypes will
be nano-adjuvanted and assessed for immunogenicity in animals (Egypt).
In summary, this initiative tackles FMDV holistically, combining field
insights, innovative stabilization techniques, and economical vaccine
development to mitigate the impact of FMDV, globally."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: British Egyptian Centre of Artifical Intelligence And Virtual hEritage technologies [BECAIVE]
descriptions:
"There is a chronic lack of technological capacity, facilities, infrastructure, and systems available to heritage authorities and archaeologists in Egypt to manage and handle the future of the use of Artificial Intelligence in the smart recording, protection and preservation of Egyptian antiquities and support new models of global tourism. With the growing influence of AI and Machine learning on the use and development of imitated copies and digital media of Egyptian antiquities, scientists and heritage professionals must develop greater awareness, critical skills, and access to digital, virtual and AI technology and methods to protect cultural heritage from piracy and illegal abuse. To this end, Egypt’s AI and machine learning protocols for its vast cultural heritage sites is in urgent need of sustainable research and technology know-how to support local professionals in scientific innovation, preservation, and protection of its hundreds of heritage sites of global significance. Those includes connecting its current heritage sites to their vast museum collections across the globe, using machine learning and AI-enabled applications and regimes for Egyptology, archaeology, museums and cultural heritage. 

The proposed project will establish an international Centre of Excellence in AI and virtual heritage technologies that will build capacity in technology acquisition, cloud-based processing, remote sensing and virtual heritage applications that support the systematic recording, monitoring, AI-enabled recognition, and digital preservation of cultural heritage sites in Egypt. The Centre adopts Professor Abdelmonem (York) ’HeritageCAVE’ award-winning conceptual framework on virtual heritage technology and activates the potential of AI and machine learning for heritage preservation in Egypt. The BECAIVE is a natural development of sustainable and long-term research partnerships between heritage authorities, research institutions and stakeholders in Egypt and the UK. The BECAIVE Centre will be run collaboratively by York and NRIAG to build capacity in (equipment, software, digital systems), knowledge exchange and training programmes."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Enhancing Educational Equity and Engagement through AI-Driven Metaverse Environments (EduSphere)
descriptions:
"This research aims to evaluate the impact of autonomous AI agents on student engagement and learning outcomes within a metaverse environment, focusing on marginalised communities in Malaysia. With the advent of Generative AI (GenAI) and metaverse technology—featuring simulations integrated with Generative Pre-trained Transformer (GPT) models, providing life-like immersive environments—there is a significant opportunity to bridge the digital divide and elevate educational engagement. The PISA 2022 results for Malaysia highlight critical gaps in student performance, particularly in creative thinking self-efficacy and science and mathematics, raising the need for innovative educational approaches. These technologies promise to transform experiential learning and offer personalised, adaptive learning experiences through autonomous AI agents.

Despite the promising potential of AI and metaverse technologies, there are gaps in our understanding of their effective implementation. Current methods for embedding GenAI into educational environments show promise but lack sophisticated models that enable dynamic AI-avatar interactions. Prior studies such as those on Embodied AI that consider cognitive and behavioural traits exist - and suggest new mechanisms to incorporate them into prompt templates. Evidence supporting the effectiveness of these technologies in educational settings is still emerging, particularly concerning their application among marginalised communities. Additionally, it is unclear how these groups, including B40 and indigenous students (i.e. bottom 40% household income groups in Malaysia), will engage with AI-driven educational content. These gaps have motivated the following research questions: How can autonomous AI agents within a metaverse environment impact student engagement in marginalised communities? What makes these AI agents appear human-like, and how can GenAI support their effectiveness in educational settings?

The study uses a mixed-methods approach, combining quantitative and qualitative data to assess the realism of the autonomous AI environment and learner engagement. It involves 1650 student-hours across five phases with at least 500 students over 22 months, including diverse educational levels and socio-economic backgrounds, such as the B40 group. Activities start with AI literacy (GPT) training, followed by on-site research at indigenous farms in Malaysia, content creation, content integration, and continuous refinement of educational content. Students will develop AI literacy skills through ChatGPT simulations, conduct hands-on local research, create and deliver content using Classlet, and refine educational content based on feedback. They will engage in simulations, quizzes, and tasks, promoting global citizenship and practical skills application. EduSphere comprises five districts: Tech District (UK) for MEMS sensors and smart agriculture, Green Zone (Malaysia) for sustainable farm planning, Cultural Quarter (Malaysia) for digital literacy, Health Plaza (UK) for rural healthcare, and Business Hub (Malaysia) for customer service skills.

Assessment will utilise both quantitative and qualitative approaches. Besides evaluating Embodied AI-related frameworks like distributed cognition and prospect theory on the autonomous environment, we will employ a virtual reality adapted Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) to measure ease of use, perceived performance, usefulness, and behavioural intent. Thematic analysis of interviews, focus groups, and observational data will provide deeper insights. The outcomes of this research will provide valuable insights into the effective integration of AI-driven educational technologies and their potential to bridge educational gaps in marginalised communities."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: DryCap: Advancing Kenya’s capabilities to effectively manage dryland carbon, biodiversity and natural resources
descriptions:
"DryCap will improve the management of dryland forests and savannas, by developing novel approaches to monitoring management interventions in an ecosystem that covers two thirds of Kenya. Drylands are an overlooked store of above- and below-ground carbon, contain a third of global biodiversity hotspots and contribute disproportionately to livelihoods, especially livestock grazing & wildlife-based economies. However, policy failure has led to ineffective land management, despite sustainable development in drylands being a Kenyan (Vision 2030), and African Union (2063 Agenda), policy priority.

In Kenya, an ambitious national policy agenda has now been articulated to restore and sustainably develop drylands (National Landscape and Ecosystem Restoration strategy, 2023 – 2032; Kenya National Agroforestry Strategy 2021 – 2030; National Forest Programme 2016-2030 and National Forest Policy 2023). To be successful and to “crowd in” private sector investment (e.g. in carbon and biodiversity credits), this agenda will require richer, more timely information about the state and trends of the drylands. This is required because many of the development challenges in the drylands involve trade-offs between biodiversity, carbon and rural livelihoods. Win-wins are possible, but require context-specific interventions that need to be informed by data. Without a step change in the quality of information about drylands, it is unlikely the new policy goals will be realised.

DryCap will help Kenya meet these data needs by developing new approaches to dryland monitoring. We build on the existing strengths of KEFRI’s long term monitoring programmes and an 8-year partnership between KEFRI and University of Edinburgh. We will develop new technologies and capacitate 5 Kenyan institutions and approx. 15 NGOs and private sector actors in their use, lowering the costs of dryland monitoring programmes and providing evidence to support better policy making. These technologies combine state-of-the-art but cost-effective laser, radar and acoustic sensors with AI-powered analysis tools. DryCap will test these novel technologies in the Kenyan context and create a hub for dryland innovation where other new technologies can be rapidly appraised, positioning KEFRI as leaders in this field. Where these approaches are found to be appropriate, we will develop a workplan so that they are incorporated into Kenyan natural resource management, including preparing for the first national forest inventory and supporting Kenyan national and international reporting. The long-term outcomes will be more effective use of the US$3.6M/year that Kenyan government institutions spend on dryland monitoring, and new opportunities for the private sector. This in turn will allow better focusing of government interventions and private sector innovation, which will lead to better environmental and social outcomes and help Kenya meet its ambitious climate, biodiversity and poverty goals for the drylands."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: " High-Purity Hydrogen Production via Catalytic Steam Pyrolysis-Reforming of Refuse-Derived Fuel (RDF) Using an Integrated Inorganic Membrane Reactor"
descriptions:
"The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), introduced as part of the European Green Deal, aims to address carbon emissions and promote environmental sustainability. By January 1, 2026, importers will be required to purchase CBAM certificates based on the carbon emissions generated during the production processes of the goods they import. This system is designed to incentivize lower carbon emissions globally.

During this transitional period, importers must report the embedded carbon emissions of imported goods considered to have a high risk of carbon leakage: steel and iron, aluminum, cement, fertilizers, electricity, and hydrogen. This reporting phase is intended to prepare importers and exporters for the upcoming certificate purchase requirements and to gather essential data on carbon emissions.

CBAM will impact the global supply chain, affecting exporters worldwide. One notable company impacted is Siam Cement Group (SCG), the largest and oldest cement producer in Southeast Asia. SCG is a pioneer in promoting a circular economy and a low-carbon society. As a member of the Global Cement and Concrete Association (GCCA), SCG shares the association’s goal of supporting sustainable economic, social, and environmental development through concrete solutions.

Since 2018, SCG has been collaborating with the Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Laboratory (https://catre.cpe.tggs.kmutnb.ac.th/) established by Professor Hartley in 2016, and CMTECH (https://catre.cpe.tggs.kmutnb.ac.th/cm-tech/) established by Professors Hartley and Professor Li in 2022. These collaborations have resulted in several successful projects funded by Thai organizations and international bodies such as the Royal Academy of Engineering (RAEng) and the European Commission’s Southeast Asia-Europe Joint Funding Scheme for Research and Innovation (JFS). These projects focus on converting carbon dioxide (CO2) into valuable chemicals such as dimethyl carbonate (DMC), renewable methane (CH4), olefins, and methanol.

Building on previous successful projects and collaborations, the current proposal aims to further decarbonize SCG’s cement industry by utilizing one of Thailand’s abundant feedstocks: Refuse-Derived Fuel (RDF), which can be sourced from municipal waste. The project proposes to study high-purity hydrogen production through catalytic steam pyrolysis of RDF using an integrated inorganic membrane reactor. The hydrogen produced can then be used in various processes to convert CO2 into valuable products. The external heat required for this process will be supplied through electrification and RDF-to-electricity conversion.

The project activities will include synthesis of hydrogen-permeable membrane, selecting the most suitable reactor, integrating the designed membrane into the reactor system, testing the process in relevant environments, with five key deliverables: (1) Identification of suitable membranes for hydrogen permeation, (2) Identification of appropriate reactors for RDF pyrolysis, (3) Development of an integrated membrane reactor for simultaneous RDF pyrolysis and purified hydrogen production, (4) Evaluation of process performance, including yield, selectivity, and hydrogen production rate, and (5) Organization of a workshop to foster collaboration among research alliances and stakeholders, as well as delivery of two membrane catalysis courses for local PhD students and young engineers.

Through these efforts, the project aims to contribute significantly to reducing carbon emissions in the cement industry, aligning with global sustainability goals and supporting the transition to a low-carbon economy."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Photocatalytic and photolectrocatalytic conversion of local feedstocks into valuable building blocks
descriptions:
"Our societies urgently need to develop methods that provide clean fuels
that do not emit greenhouse gas emissions and we need to reduce our
reliance on chemical building blocks that are derived from oil and gas.
Developing processes that provide these building blocks allows for the
deep decarbonisation of the chemical industry, which significant
greenhouse gas emissions and provide essential products and materials
essential for our societies.
A particular exciting opportunity arises from the use of local feedstocks that
are currently unused by upcycling these into chemical building blocks
coupled with the production of hydrogen. This reduces not only the
dependency on the import of chemicals, but also results in opportunities for
the development of the local economy, and reduced greenhouse gas
emissions.
In this project we will combine the strengths of the team at the University of
Strathclyde in photocatalysis (PC) using conjugated polymers with
Chulalongkorn University' team in flow systems, photoelectrocatalysis
(PEC), and metal oxides/sulfides for oxidation chemistry and hydrogen
production. Together, we will develop new PC and PEC systems for the
selective conversion of a local feedstock (molasses, sugars) into useful
chemical intermediates in Thailand, with the simultaneous production of
hydrogen as a green fuel using sunlight to drive the process. Comparing
the performances of a range of materials in parallel will allow us to gain
much more detailed understanding as both PC and PEC are inherently
related. This will also allow us to design better materials through feedback
loops in the project and going forward in new projects. Exchange of staff
and PhD students will facilitate the work together with local partners in
Thailand, i.e. a chemical company (SCGC), a sugar company (KSL) and
local feedstock producers. Local engagement with communities through
outreach will further the impact of the project by promoting STEM and UN
SDGs."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Social Finance for Better Post-Disaster Health
descriptions:
"Over the past 20 years, Indonesia has recorded over 24,000 disaster
events that caused 190,500 fatalities, displaced almost 37 million people
and caused extensive injury, disability and mental health damage to those
who were affected. Much of the immediate physical health effects such as
type and extent of injury, mental health impacts and effects on household
health spending are not systematically documented. The longer-term
effects of disasters on health and household health costs are still less
known. Moreover, existing programs solely focus on alleviating immediate
impact of disaster rather than longer-term health impacts. None of this lack
of data, lack of understanding of effects beyond the immediate aftermath or
short-term policy focus are unique to Indonesia.
This project will initiate a new research and innovation collaboration
between researchers in the UK and Indonesia, that looks at health
consequences beyond the immediate aftermath of disaster, and the
feasibility of implementing innovative health financing to support better
longer-term post-disaster health of those affected.
We will use secondary longitudinal survey data complemented by machine
learning methods, and wider literature, to understand short and longer-term
health consequences of disasters. This understanding, together with
community-level case studies and interviews with relevant experts, will be
used to assess the feasibility of designing and implementing innovative
social finance instruments modelled around outcome-based contracting (a
form of results-based financing) to support better health, post-disaster.
Collaborating with the Ministry of National Development Planning, Ministry
of Social Affairs and the Social Insurance agency, the project will suggest
how the findings can be integrated into the current social protection
programme in Indonesia, and identify new, policy relevant research
collaborations, to create significant, lasting impact pathways."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Combating Antimicrobial Resistance with Cutting-Edge Synergistic Ozone and Laser Technology Enhanced by Probiotic Surface Treatment
descriptions:
Microbial systems are complex and can have both beneficial and unwanted effects on co-existing organisms. For humans, the development of resistant microbes is inevitable, causing a global concern that warrants innovative solutions. This project proposes a novel approach to reduce antimicrobial resistance (AMR) through the synergistic use of ozone and lasers to decontaminate environmental surfaces, followed by re-colonization with beneficial microbial systems. The aim is to provide a comprehensive and effective solution to the growing problem of AMR, which has significant implications for public health and the economy.
Environmental surfaces, especially in healthcare settings, are critical points for the spread of infections. Effective decontamination of these surfaces is essential to prevent transmission of pathogens. This project will explore the synergistic effects of ozone and laser technologies to achieve thorough and efficient surface decontamination. Ozone, a powerful and eco-friendly oxidant, will be applied in both gas and aqueous forms, including ozone mist, to ensure sterile conditions. Lasers, particularly UV lasers, will complement this process by disinfecting surfaces from a safe distance. The combination of these technologies aims to optimize the decontamination process, ensuring that all areas, including those difficult to reach with traditional methods, are effectively treated. A key aspect of this project is the investigation of using beneficial microbial systems to prevent the re-colonization of pathogens on decontaminated surfaces. We will explore whether extracellular compounds produced by the microbiota can inhibit the growth of harmful bacteria. This approach not only reduces the need for ongoing antimicrobial use but also promotes the establishment of a healthy microbial environment. By preventing the re-establishment of pathogens, we aim to create a sustainable solution that minimizes the risk of infection and AMR spread. Our objectives include optimizing the concentration, time, and dose of ozone and laser applications to maximize their effectiveness. We will conduct rigorous testing in both laboratory settings and simulated hospital environments to ensure the reliability and efficacy of the proposed method. Additionally, we will analyse the impact of probiotic treatments in maintaining a beneficial microbial balance on surfaces. The potential impact of this project extends beyond academia. In the short to medium term, the outcomes will benefit various stakeholders, including healthcare providers, patients, and the broader community. By providing a more efficient and eco-friendly method of decontamination, we aim to reduce healthcare-associated infections, lower the burden on healthcare systems, and improve patient outcomes. The reduction in AMR will also have significant economic benefits by decreasing the need for expensive antimicrobial treatments and reducing the incidence of infection-related complications. This collaborative effort between the University of the West of Scotland and Laser Institute for Research and Applications in Egypt leverages the extensive expertise developed in both institutions. The project is expected to produce high-impact publications and foster further international research partnerships. By addressing a critical global health challenge, this research aligns with several Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), including SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-being), SDG 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation), and SDG 15 (Life on Land).

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Designating Tropical Important Plant Areas: towards conserving Papua's forests to secure future healthy populations
descriptions:
"New Guinea is the world's floristically most diverse island. Papua Barat, the
Indonesian province located on the Bird's Head of New Guinea, is a
'conservation province', with a declaration to conserve 70% of its forest
cover. This project will use the Tropical Important Plant Areas (TIPAs)
conservation framework to assess three botanically poorly known areas
based on their species composition, and threats to the health of their plant
populations. Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, will work together with the
Regional Research and Innovation Agency, West Papua and Universitas
Papua to make three expeditions to botanically poorly known areas. Each
will gather botanical collections and record habitat observations and
permanent forest plots. Botanical collections will provide invaluable data for
taxonomists to verify the species present and increase species occurrence
data lacking for these areas. Habitat observations will provide evidence
required on the threats to species' habitat in the IUCN Red Listing workflow
to assess species' conservation status. The forest plots established will be
used for future monitoring and training for students, staff and indigenous
communities in vegetation survey techniques. Training will ensure plant
specimens collected are curated to a high standard, maintaining them as
future tools for research. A workshop at the 2025 Flora Malesiana
symposium will consolidate relationships with local and national
government departments and NGOs that will be necessary to ensure areas
designated as TIPAs are considered in conservation planning. This is
important in Papua Barat, as it faces challenges of poverty and low HDI,
with pressure mounting for spatial development. We will engage with
indigenous communities during our expeditions through materials and
activities specifically designed to include people of different genders and
ages in the process towards conserving the forest ecosystems which are
the foundation of healthy future populations."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Developing porous adsorbents for lithium recovery from subsurface brines: investigating diffusion and adsorption processes
descriptions: Lithium recovery from subsurface brines such as geothermal brines, is becoming more important to enable supplying the forecasted global demand for this mineral in the coming decades. Adsorption by functionalized (ion-exchange) materials is among the promising processes for lithium extraction. Nevertheless, the cost of adsorbents and extended residence time required for brines in such adsorption processes (normally 10-24 hours), combined with the low lithium concentration (typically 10-200 mg/L), hamper economic efficiency of lithium recovery from geothermal brines. Therefore, there is a need for developing long lasting ion-exchange compound materials with high adsorption rate and capacity. In this research project, we propose to use graphene oxide (GO) in a titanium oxide-based compound adsorbent, along with polyethylene glycol (PEG) to provide a solution for the above challenges. GO monolayers are expected to attract lithium ions toward the ion-exchange sites on surfaces through the negative charges around the oxygen-containing groups. PEG will generate pore spaces within the structure of compound materials leading to higher surface area and hence increase the lithium adsorption capacity. Both batch and continuous flow experiments will be used to measure the effectiveness of lithium ion-exchange adsorbent in the compound materials and their ion selectivity performance. Furthermore, porous pellets with different porosity and flat sheet membranes will be fabricated. The optimum composition of adsorbent materials will then be used in dynamic flow experiments (adsorption column for granules and flat sheet membrane module for membrane sheets) under the same operational conditions i.e., flowrate, temperature, feed concentration among others. By using modelling tools, we will explore the significance of ion diffusion and porosity of materials, and their interaction with other variables (flow and operational variables such as velocity of fluid and concentration of feed) during lithium recovery from brines and propose an optimised structure for new ion-exchange compound materials. The outcomes of the project will provide new materials/insights to recover lithium from geothermal brines and enhance the economic sustainability of the Indonesia’s geothermal resources. Therefore, by contributing to the supply of lithium for modern technologies, the project’s success will expedite achieving Indonesia’s geothermal power capacity target of 9,300 megawatts by 2035, as indicated by the government, by attracting and justifying investments. Furthermore, it supports the country’s energy transition plans and its economy, and eventually contribute to the welfare of the society. Upon the success of the project, the associated partner of the project will work with the project leads (UK-Indonesia) to explore opportunities to secure financial support for field trial of the proposed method and materials in their fields (a medium-term impact of the project). Through this project, project leaders (UK and Indonesian) will build a strong collaboration to enable them to target research studies in sustainable energy area through their expertise (UoA: modelling of flow and diffusion/adsorption processes, and Diponegoro University: expertise in design/fabrication of membranes). Furthermore, early career researchers will be involved in this international project where the industry and public engagements along with scientific discussions, prepare them for being future independent researchers (capacity developments as short-term individual level impacts).

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Climate Resilient Energy Efficient Low-income Housing in Egypt (CRLiH)
descriptions:
"Developing countries in tropical and sub-tropical regions will be hit the
worst by climate change. In Egypt, for instance, average annual
temperatures are expected to increase by 2.1°C by 2050, and by 4.4°C by
the end of the century, with the frequency and intensity of heat waves also
expected to increase. Rising external temperatures significantly increase
the risk of overheating, cooling load, energy consumption, and associated
carbon emissions in buildings. Poor building design and quality also
contribute to excessive energy consumption as well as to critical thermal
discomfort which may lead to heat exhortation, heat syncope or heat
stroke, with the vulnerable groups including children and older occupants of
buildings most as risk. Because of their vulnerable living conditions and the
limited access to appropriate/adequate infrastructure, low-income
populations from the low and medium HDI countries would suffer more
from the effects of the climate change. The low level of awareness
combined with the limited ability of the low-income people to adapt to
climate change, make the situation even more critical. Unlike the rich
countries who have the resources to adapt to climate change, adaptation in
many developing countries is left to the individuals as a matter of
""self-help"". The current situation will disproportionately affect the living
standards and health and wellbeing of low-income populations the majority
of whom live in substandard low-quality homes. Particular attention should
therefore be paid to the low-income housing conditions not only to address
the environmental concerns but also to improve the living standards and
health and wellbeing of low-income people to increase their resilience to
long-term environmental risks posed by the climate change. To this end,
the CRLiH project intends to identify, develop, and then assess low-cost
climate-proof retrofit strategies, to reduce energy consumptions and risk of
overheating in low-income housing in Egypt."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: RESIBUILD: Resilient Buildings Innovated through AI-supported Design and Easy Manufacturing
descriptions:
"We will create the first AI-powered 'virtual engineer' tool for the integrated
design of resilient, digitally manufactured, and sustainable houses for
seismic areas in Turkey.
Our vision is to achieve the seamless co-creation of structures whose
layouts and structural dimensioning is carried out by AI software interacting
with end users of limited technical knowledge.
This tool will deliver construction plans for optimized components of
minimal carbon footprint made from CNC-cut plates of wood-based panels
(plywood) and moulded Glass Fibre Reinforced Concrete (GFRC) panels
that can be easily assembled by small teams without the need for
traditional construction skills.
The project will produce: i) an AI software engine interfacing with a
user-friendly app that generates optimal designs of (one-storey but
expandable) houses based on simple user inputs (areas, room
configuration, etc.), ii) a verified workflow and manufacturing protocol from
design to final assembly, iii) a proof-of-concept prototype to be constructed
at full-scale and tested to destruction (to verify its earthquake resistance).
The technology will target the communities displaced by the recent
earthquakes in Turkey, who are still in need of safe permanent habitable
spaces. However, the research programme and training initiated by the
project can have far reaching implications in the state of the art of modular
housing design-manufacture-assembly both in Turkey and the UK.
The optimization process will incorporate local environmental and
sustainability constraints and will open the door for small, local fabricators
to share design solutions and will build local economic capacity.
To do this, we bring together experts on: AI informed structural design and
timber (Imperial), digital and parametric fabrication of bespoke GFRC
panels (Fibrobeton), and local researchers with deep knowledge of the
constraints and needs of seismically affected areas (Bursa)."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Advancing Türkiye and UK Midwives' Research Capacity Through Research Skills Training, Networking, Pump-priming, and Mentorship
descriptions:
Maternal and infant health remains a critical development challenge in Türkiye, with significant implications for economic development and social welfare. Despite healthcare investments, substantial disparities persist: maternal mortality rates are 14.6 per 100,000 live births and infant mortality rates are 9.0 per 1,000 live births (Turkish Statistical Institute, 2025; World Health Organisation, 2025)—significantly exceeding EU averages and more than double UK rates. Eastern provinces show even higher maternal mortality (Çim et al., 2017), where accessing quality care is particularly challenging. 
By training 12 Turkish midwives in evidence-based research methods, the programme creates a skilled workforce capable of developing locally-relevant interventions to reduce these preventable deaths.
The root cause is insufficient evidence-based maternity care, stemming from minimal midwifery research capacity. Türkiye has only 25 midwifery professors across 67 universities (YÖK Academic Search, 2025). Turkish midwives lack accessible pathways to research training: Masters and PhD programmes exist in limited universities without part-time options, excluding working clinicians. Research output remains overwhelmingly Turkish-language, preventing international knowledge exchange (Öztürk et al., 2018). Clinical midwives receive no support translating evidence into practice.
Our proposed activities directly address these barriers through clear pathways to impact:• Research Capacity Building → Improved Care → Better Outcomes: Training 24 midwives (12 Turkish) in research methods creates a cohort capable of conducting locally-relevant studies. UK collaboration ensures international standards whilst maintaining cultural appropriateness. These midwives will identify context-specific solutions to reduce mortality in their communities.
• International Teams → Sustainable Partnerships → Knowledge Transfer: All pump-primed teams include UK and Turkish members, ensuring bidirectional learning. UK midwives share established research methodologies; Turkish midwives provide essential cultural and contextual understanding. This exchange produces research addressing real Turkish healthcare challenges whilst meeting international quality standards.
• Open-Access Resources → Widespread Adoption → System Change: Bilingual training materials enable hundreds more Turkish midwives to develop research skills without expensive international travel. This democratises access to research training, particularly benefiting midwives in underserved eastern provinces.
• Mentorship → External Funding → Scaled Impact: Six-month mentorship positions teams for major grant success. External funding enables larger studies directly improving maternal care protocols, potentially saving hundreds of lives annually.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Sustainable Ethical Cattle from Antiquity to the Anthropocene
descriptions:
"Cattle farming is often viewed as environmentally and climatically harmful.
Sustainable beef production is possible, but it requires the adoption of
certain animal and land management practices, ideally semi-intensive
silvopastoralism. Türkiye produces and consumes many cattle but has thus
far avoided using large-scale feedlots, a method that causes the greatest
environmental harm. As the country continues to modernize, and demand
for beef rises, practices are shifting away from sustainable and resilient
small-scale household livestock management. Archaeological evidence
from the Bronze Age to Late Antiquity indicates that historically, people
favoured beef, yet respected the carry capacity of the landscape.
This project combines multi-isotopic analyses with ethnographic research
to better understand how Türkiye, and especially the region of the
Morsynus river valley, historically supported large numbers of cattle.
Isotope analysis from cattle bones and teeth from the Late Antique city of
Aphrodisias will reveal herding practices, diet, and breeding patterns, while
analysis of archaeobotanical material will determine crop watering and
manuring practices. As a region highly suited to cattle production, we
hypothesize that Aphrodisias was the main supplier of cows to Western
Anatolia. Conversations with communities connected to the site, many of
whom still keep livestock, will explore and record changes in contemporary
animal management practices. The project will result in the publication of a
white paper, providing advice to policy makers, governments, and the
public. In-person training workshops at Koç University (Istanbul) and
Aphrodisias will increase in-country capacity for isotopic work, allowing for
further environmental and climatic research. This collaboration between
archaeologists, ethnographers and local communities will lead to creative
outputs that raise awareness of ancient and contemporary practices that
may inform the future of cattle farming."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: SPEAR- Solar powered electroporator for freshwater purification in Jordan based refugee-camps
descriptions: This ISPF collaboration will build on previous collaboration between GJU and GCU, the two institutions have common interests in multidisciplinary research related to climate changes and tackling issues that are societally important to improve people’s life and support communities. This collaboration will pave the road for working closely and exchange knowledge in areas where both teams have excelled and accumulated expertise in. The Jordanian government is implementing community-led initiatives and infrastructure projects to help communities adapt to climate change impacts, such as water scarcity. The government is also working to strengthen primary healthcare and improve access to quality healthcare services, social protection, human capital development, and economic empowerment. The intended collaboration will be focusing on supplying remote villages in Jordan with clean water, which is increasingly becoming a great concern, the case study will be implemented in the vicinity of Wadi Al Arab, where the sources of water are diverse, including the King Abdallah Canal. The source water quality varies significantly, some of the challenges include high turbidity, bacteria, and organic content. The water supply systems in Wadi Al Arab area support several communities including high percentage of vulnerable refugees. The teams will develop power electronics- based circuit that purifies the supply water to almost 100%, that reduces the dependency on the typical purification process using Chlorine, the developed technique has tremendous advantages, particularly in high organic content water. The research includes developing controlled signals with calculated frequency and electric field strength that kills the microorganisms and purify water sample. The energy required to generate those control signals will be harvested from the solar irradiance which is quite rich in Jordan in general and specially in the northern parts where the implementation will be carried out. This will reduce the dependency on the grid connection, thus creating a more sustainable solution, that would also help reduce the CO2 footprint. GCU team has the experiences in developing controlled electric field for water and cancer treatments, this will enhance the overall knowledge of the two teams. As can be evidenced, the collaboration outcomes are expected to help the Energy and Water supply sectors in Jordan. It will also tackle serious health issues, that satisfies the UN SDGs #3 for good health through affording clean water. UN SDGs #6 through good health leading to lowering poverty. UN SDGs #1, where people can install and run PV systems for their usage, and earn income. Using solar power is a target of this project, it capitalises on the availability of renewable sources in the area without stressing the country grid, it also assures reducing CO2 footprint, thus addressing UN SDGs #7. Water companies will benefit from the project outcomes as this is expected to reduce the Chlorine used in conventional purifications stations, which in turn has an economical advantage in addition to lowering the risks associated with chlorinating high organic matter water. Nationwide, with the project succession, other districts in Jordan can adopt the developed system and publicising its benefits, which satisfies UN SDGs # 11.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Addressing the challenges of diagnosis of human malaria, towards elimination in Indonesia by 2030
descriptions:
"Human malaria is a serious infectious disease caused by five different parasite types, and is a serious health challenge, especially to children and pregnant women. Many countries in the world are attempting to eliminate malaria by 2030, thereby meeting one of the World Health Organisation’s Sustainable Development Goals. Indonesia, a country on the DAC list of ODA recipients, had nearly half a million malaria cases and over 2000 deaths at the last survey. Good progress has been made in recent years towards the goal of malaria elimination by 2030, but progress has now stalled.

To eliminate malaria, infection must be diagnosed accurately, and treated with an effective drug. Diagnosis is by microscopy, or a specific rapid dipstick test known as an RDT. Almost half of malaria cases in Indonesia are diagnosed by RDT. However new parasites circulating globally have evolved so that the existing RDT no longer detect them. Many countries are carrying out surveys to find out if these parasites have established there, but these require advanced laboratory tools. In addition, a type of malaria that usually infects monkeys is being found in humans in SE Asia, possibly as a result of deforestation activity. These infections cannot be detected by any of the current diagnostic tools being used in Indonesia; again advanced laboratory tools are needed.

The collaboration between the University of Glasgow and Universitas Indonesia aims to solve these diagnostic challenges for Indonesia, which threaten its ability to control and eliminate malaria. We will train intensively a researcher from Indonesia in the molecular techniques, and then transfer the technology and skills to Universitas Indonesia. Once established, these molecular tests will then be applied to samples from patients with suspected malaria. We will examine patient samples collected from two sites in Indonesia, which are widely-separated geographically. By applying the new molecular tools, we will be able to establish if the two new types of malaria circulate in these Indonesian regions. We will also compare the accuracy of microscopy, RDT and the new molecular tools to diagnose malaria, and to identify the two new types of malaria.

If we do find evidence of the two new types of malaria parasite, we will inform the relevant malaria control bodies within Indonesia, who can then take steps to improve malaria diagnosis, by applying molecular tests, or developing new ones. At the same time, we will raise awareness with health workers of the possibility that malaria infections may be missed by the currently-used methods, and provide addtiional trainings in the new diagnostic methods. The overall aim is to improve malaria diagnosis so that the ultimate goal of malaria elimination can be met.
Finally we will provide the information to the World Health Organisation, who are mapping the occurrence of these new malaria types that threaten control and elimination.
Eliminating malaria will have strong societal and economic benefits. The results of this study will contribute to better diagnosis, management, and control of malaria, which will reduce personal and national health cost / spending on malaria."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Earthquake Awareness for Architectural Heritage Preservation - RESILIENT
descriptions: Turkiye is one of the most important regions worldwide regarding cultural and archaeological heritage, with 21 UNESCO World Heritage sites. However, this cultural heritage is in high-seismic areas and at constant risk of being severely damaged or irremediably lost, as demonstrated by the recent 2023-Turkiye/Syria Earthquake that killed over 50,000 people, destroying over 150 cultural heritage buildings with over $100 billion of damage (https://news.un.org/en/story/2023/04/1135532). Simultaneously, Turkiye is one of the countries more severely exposed to climate change, due to its geographical location in the Eastern Mediterranean Basin region (Güler-Kumar,2022), exacerbating material degradation and geotechnical hazards, resulting in an increased seismic vulnerability of historical constructions. These combined effects make climate change in cultural-heritage seismic regions a complex-multidisciplinary issue with potentially significant socioeconomic consequences. In addition to the loss of human life and negative impact on economic sectors like tourism, the loss of cultural-heritage assets irremediably affects the historical identity and traditions of the local communities where these structures are located, representing a valuable immaterial heritage that needs to be preserved. The correct perception and awareness of seismic risk associated with historic constructions are fundamental prerequisites to establishing an authentic culture of seismic prevention in cultural heritage sites. On the contrary, the long return periods that often characterise catastrophic earthquakes lead to underestimating seismic risk by people and authorities, and losing the seismic-protection culture gained after previous devastating events, making communities prepared for proactive measures to protect their architectural and cultural heritage. In this regard, only a holistic vision of this global challenge supported by interdisciplinary skills across social and engineering sciences can provide local communities with the necessary background to understand how cultural heritage is vulnerable and how its preservation can positively impact their community's life. RESILIENT aims to increase awareness of seismic risk in local communities and policymakers in earthquake-prone historic areas of Turkiye, driving vernacular practices for a culture of seismic-prevention led by people’s everyday actions. The project will adopt a transdisciplinary methodology linking social science, engineering and digital-cultural-heritage skills to predict and reduce tangible and intangible cultural-heritage losses due to earthquake events. The research will involve numerical simulations to identify combined geotechnical-structural criticisms in cultural heritage assets and predict potential damage scenarios; and social research to understand community's spatial and social connection to heritage sites and assess the barriers and enablers that influence readiness for disasters. RESILIENT will be intersectoral, involving public sector (local authorities), private sector (tourism operators), and local communities to ensure effective two-way communication and knowledge transfer between academia and society, and will receive the support of nationally relevant stakeholders managing local cultural associations, maximising the societal impact. RESILIENT will contribute to reducing economic, social, and cultural losses due to future earthquakes, significantly increasing the quality of life in Turkish society, and meeting the UN-SGs, particularly UN-SG11:"Sustainable Cities and Communities" (https://turkiye.un.org/en/sdgs/11). RESILIENT will establish new research and innovation collaborations among Atilim, METU and Durham Universities, strengthening the international role of the two leaders in the worldwide strategic field of cultural heritage preservation.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Climate-Resilient Railways: Advanced Monitoring of Railway Ballast Degradation under Climate Change Influences
descriptions: Turkey’s railway system has seen remarkable growth, [with an 85.59 percent increase in passenger transport volume in 2022, reaching 19.8 billion passenger-kilometers.](https://www.statista.com/statistics/437107/passengers-transported-by-rail-in-turkey-in-million-passenger-kilometres/#:~:text=The%20annual%20transport%20volume%20of%20passenger%20trains%20in,in%202022%20in%20comparison%20to%20the%20previous%20year.) This highlights its critical role in the nation’s infrastructure. However, climate change poses significant challenges to this vital system, as identified by the [World Bank](https://www.worldbank.org/en/country/turkey/brief/key-highlights-country-climate-and-development-report-for-turkiyehttps://), due to Turkey’s high vulnerability to climate-related disruptions. Climate-related disruptions such as flood hazards pose significant physical threats to urban transport systems, potentially leading to substantial loss of life and considerable financial damage.   To protect this essential infrastructure, it is crucial to implement advanced warning systems that monitor the critical elements of the railway. Accordingly, this project aims to develop an advanced warning system and experimentally test it using an element of railway-track substructure combined with climate change models, developing strategies to make railways more resilient.   This proactive approach not only enhances safety and reliability but also optimizes maintenance resources, making it a key step towards sustainable transport infrastructure in the face of changing environmental conditions. Addressing this critical issue aligns with the concept of a resilient planet and necessitates the development of robust solution methodologies to mitigate material losses and casualties due to climate change events.   This collaboration will bring together world class researchers from the Institute of Railway Research, University of Huddersfield, with extensive experience in railway research and the Akdeniz University team with extensive experience in hydraulic research. The two teams will work together to develop experimental setup and data collection process.   A scaled railway substructure model will be designed in an open channel facility with adjustable flow parameters simulating different flood scenarios. The flood scenarios will be designed to mimic the impact of various climate related events. Sensors’ systems will be implemented to monitor the elements railway substructure model and record the degradation in real-time. The collected data will be used in developing machine learning models to evaluate the impact of various climate change events on the degradation patterns of a railway substructure element, allowing for more accurate predictions and timely maintenance.   The project will study the ballast layer, a railway substructure of small irregular stones surround conventional railway tracks, which holds rails and sleepers in place, resists train forces, improves passenger comfort, and limits damage. Ballast allows track adjustments through tamping and is vital for safety. Extreme weather, like floods, can damage ballast, making tracks unsafe and increasing derailment risk. For example, Storm Ciara washed away ballast on the Conwy Valley line in Wales, causing significant disruption and costing £2.2m of repairs to reopen. The project aims to understand ballast’s vulnerability to wear and tear from climate change-related weather events.  The outcomes of this project, in the shorter term, will provide guidance to railway engineers in designing and maintaining ballasted railway tracks under flooding conditions and enhance the understanding of the ballast layer’s discharge mechanisms. In the longer term, the project is a significant step toward using warning systems in conditions monitoring and creating a digital twin railway system by defining the necessary requirement for such a system.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Reimagining digital mobility platforms: co-designing gender-responsive and care-aware mobility solutions
descriptions: Imagine a mobile app that not only gives directions from A to B but also suggests the safest route, less crowded buses, accessible stations, grocery shops, or playgrounds when travelling with children, and rest areas for when you need a break or are accompanying an older relative. While these features may seem basic, they are not integrated into digital mobility platforms that optimise routes for an idealised user. This highlights a gap between digital transport technologies and the everyday realities of diverse users, which this project seeks to address by exploring what needs to be optimised, and for whom. Navigating a city can be challenging, especially for individuals with intersecting social and demographic disadvantages, whose mobility needs are often overlooked by authorities. Women are disproportionately affected due to social reproduction burdens, concerns around transport safety and personal security, cultural codes, and physical constraints during pregnancy. Evidence from Istanbul, the focus of this research, demonstrates that women feel less safe on public transport and have concerns about security both during the day and at night. They also lack confidence and independence in navigating the city. This project argues that gender-mainstreaming digital mobility platforms can address these issues while deepening discussions on gender-responsive transport planning, as catalysts for inclusive transport systems.   Drawing on the theme of ‘transformative technologies’, this research proposes a care-centred and gender-responsive redesign of digital mobility infrastructure. It aims to identify policy and design gaps and prototype AI-informed tools that support inclusive, equitable transport planning. The project brings together researchers from transport geography, computational science and creative technologies at the University of the West of England, Bristol, and geospatial engineering experts at Gebze Technical University, Turkiye. This partnership will explore innovative technological solutions to address barriers faced by women and other underrepresented gender and age groups within Istanbul’s transport system.  The research objectives are to; •   Map and analyse gender-sensitive and care-related mobility in selected Istanbul neighbourhoods through participatory methods. •   Co-design a “care-aware and gender-sensitive routing” tool for digital platforms and produce a prototype for user testing. •   Enhance local capacity for gender-inclusive transport planning by involving municipal departments and stakeholders from the diagnosis to co-design phase, broadening policy implications beyond technological solutions. •   Establish a sustainable partnership between Turkish and British partners to enable long-term collaboration, future cross-country comparisons, and the scaling of app development.  While technology is at the heart of this proposal, its ambitions extend beyond innovation. By raising awareness of gendered inequalities in transport, the project aims to foster systemic change, transforming transport and public spaces into gender-responsive environments, aligning with the UN’s Gender Equality SDG (Goal 5) and enabling women’s economic participation in the longer term. In the medium term, the project will prototype a mobility app for local authority adoption, offering customisable travel options for women and other users with diverse needs, contributing to Sustainable Cities and Communities (Goal 11). In the short term, it will deliver context-specific, gender- and care-aware mobility indicators, alongside a transferable framework, supporting future digital innovation and infrastructure partnerships (Goal 9).

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Tomorrow's Legal Talent: A New Judicial Science Curriculum for Kenya
descriptions:
"Building on longstanding professional relationships between its partners,
this co-created initiative will bring together partners at Kabarak Law School,
the Kenya Judiciary Academy, the Katiba (Constitution) Institute, and
Cardiff Law School to develop for the first time a curriculum in Judicial
Science. Kenya's judiciary is widely held to be one of the most thoroughly
reformed of the country's institutions. Under the 2010 Constitution, it has
responsibility for a range of transformative provision from the realisation of
social and economic rights to the exercise of judicial independence. Under
this new dispensation, the jurisprudence of Kenya's senior judiciary
including its new Supreme Court has come to the centre of global
constitutional studies. Three Kenyan institutions have been central to this:
founded in 2010 Kabarak Law School is now considered the country's most
progressive legal studies centres, the Judiciary Academy (formerly the
Judicial Studies Institute) has shown excellent leadership in all levels of
judicial training, and the Katiba Institute co-founded by the drafter of
Kenya's 2010 Constitution and Chair of its Constitutional Review
Commission, Prof Yash Pal Ghai FBA, has made a definitive contribution to
the country's practice of constitutional litigation. The proposed project will
bring together three generations of legal scholars and practitioners to
develop a new Masters curriculum in Judicial Science. This is a vital
development for Kenya. It will nurture tomorrow's legal talent by supporting
new and existing members of the judiciary at all levels to put into practice
the constitutional values that are central to the 2010 charter, promoting
peace, good governance, inclusion, and the rule of law. Organised around
four work packages, new course materials will be jointly developed and
tested which will enable a new curriculum to be rolled out in the 2027-2028
Kenyan academic year (which begins in January)."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Paddy-IoT: Community Prototype and Monitoring of Real-Time Agri-Paddy Hydroponics System Integrating Controlled Air Capture
descriptions: Since the 14th General Election in 2018, Malaysia has faced significant political instability resulting from multiple government changes over five years. This instability, compounded by the COVID-19 pandemic and climate change, has led to food insecurity affecting approximately 30% of the global population, primarily due to travel restrictions, food sanctions, and climate change. In 2022, India, the biggest rice exporter (40% global trade) ceased exporting broken rice and has imposed a 20% duty on rice exports caused by uneven monsoon rains and price inflation of fertilisers; to some extent also resulting from the Ukraine-Russia war. These changes significantly amplified the purchasing price on Malaysian imported food to accommodate the food needs, especially on staple food. Aggravating this is when Malaysian Ringgit went weaken by the end of 2023 and the beginning of 2024. All these factors have severely impacted on Malaysian economy, causing inflation on their general food and living costs. Therefore, it is an urgent need for Malaysia to focus on enhancing its food security, particularly agri-food (agricultural food) industry. In history, Malaysia’s long-serving previous government had always been prioritised commodity plantation and manufacturing industries for their high revenue contribution to the national Gross Domestic Products (GDP), led to marginalising agri-food industry. Changing status of agricultural land to industrial land (for manufacturing) in previous has now caused very limited land available for agri-food farming and production. Due to this circumstance, one effective solution is by exploiting the use of hydroponics farming system, which allows soilless cropping to be in place, thus avoiding deforestation and will limit the land requisition for agriculture. However, implementing hydroponics presents challenges, such as plant diseases and requiring balanced nutrient levels and controlling factors like water pH and temperature. To address all these challenges, innovating and prototyping a small-scale high-precision smart paddy hydroponics growth with real-time monitoring system for indoor application is proposed, targeting the technology readiness level (TRL) of 4 or 5. This novel system will be explored by designing the engineering (hardware) parts of a grow tent consisting of closed-loop fertigation (fertiliser mixed with irrigation) pipelines, water tank, fertiliser tank, paddy bed (rack), actuators, and environmental sensors. To enable its automation, a system architecture adopting nonlinear dynamic control model will be designed and programmed. Meanwhile adopting deep learning convolutional neural network model enables data monitoring, prediction and visualisation by integrating the main system with IoT protocols, cloud platform, and mobile app. This ambitious IoT agri-paddy hydroponics growth and monitoring system will transform the Malaysian conventional paddy cultivation by researching its viability to cultivate more than twice a year within a controlled environment. Additionally, integrating carbon sequestration utilising an inline duct fan, inspired by photosynthesis, enhances the system’s novelty in terms of decarbonising the environment. Finally, the benefits of the proposed innovation will be shared with targeted communities, of university students as the pilot participants engaging with the smart farming prototype, urban residents, Malaysian government agency of Department of Agriculture (DOA), and a charity organisation that houses the underrepresented group, of Rumah Melor.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Advancing Solar-Thermal Micro-Scale Power Systems with Integrated Energy Storage
descriptions: This project brings together researchers from the University of Hertfordshire (UK) and the University of Pretoria (South Africa) to address a shared challenge: how to make small-scale solar power systems more practical, efficient, and reliable, particularly for communities with limited or no access to the electricity grid. The focus is on solar-thermal technology, specifically a system that employs a solar dish to drive a micro-scale Brayton cycle engine integrated with thermal energy storage. While this configuration shows considerable promise, it continues to face technical challenges, particularly in its ability to respond effectively to fluctuating environmental conditions throughout the day. Our collaboration aims to address these limitations directly. This work directly addresses South Africa’s rural energy access challenge, where millions of people still lack reliable electricity. It aligns with the country’s National Development Plan 2030 and renewable energy strategies, supporting the deployment of decentralised, low‑carbon micro‑grids for under‑served communities. By strengthening local research capacity and providing tools for practical system design, the project offers a credible pathway to real‑world impact within 3–10 years. The project’s core objective is to develop and evaluate a comprehensive simulation model that captures both steady-state performance and the system’s dynamic behaviour. By analysing how the system responds to variations in solar input, load demand, and thermal storage scenarios, we aim to optimise control strategies that enhance operational stability and energy efficiency under real-world conditions. This dynamic modelling and control development is a critical step toward viable, deployable solutions. The partnership leverages complementary expertise: the UK team’s strengths in simulation and system optimisation, and South Africa’s experimental capabilities in solar dish–Brayton systems. Together, we will tailor the model to reflect South African solar conditions and practical design constraints, establishing a platform for scalable applications in other high-solar-resource regions. A central component of the project is capacity building for early-career researchers. Through joint training sessions, collaborative workshops, and academic exchange, the project will provide young engineers and researchers with hands-on experience in advanced tools for clean energy systems, simulation, and control. This initiative is not only about solving technical problems; it is equally focused on building long-term capability and strengthening research partnerships between the two institutions. The anticipated impact extends beyond academia. Individually, the project will support the professional development of emerging researchers. Institutionally, it will enhance expertise and foster sustainable collaboration. More broadly, the project contributes to global goals such as expanding access to clean, affordable energy, fostering innovation in low-carbon technologies, and enhancing climate resilience. In the longer term, the outcomes of this work could inform real-world pilot projects and support energy planning in regions with abundant solar resources but limited infrastructure. By establishing the technical foundations and control strategies for a flexible, solar-thermal micro power system, this project takes a meaningful step toward delivering reliable, locally adapted, and sustainable energy solutions.
